The Emperor bestowed his favor upon both paths; Xuanzang and Daosheng were the two eminent patriarchs. Xin-xing wept over the ox;
Tan-you knocked on the tiger’s door. Hui-chi [faced] Longmen; Zhu Fa-qian lived in a thatched hut and carried jade out from the clouds.

Shenhuang was the Master of Treatises. Lingrun contemplated fire; Zhikai vowed by a pond. Minggong ate deer;

Zhicang sat majestically upon his seat; Dao’an ascended his carriage. Fakai possessed literary brilliance; Tanyan excelled in quick-witted eloquence.
Daozheng transcended the mundane; Zhicheng entered the realm of goodness. At Nanyang, the pheasant and the dove [were reconciled];

Tanping’s voice was majestic. Senghui were two heroes; Mingyan were three paragons.
Fatong possessed great strength; Daokai walked with vigor. Puhua leaned on a wooden staff; Master Xiang dug a pit.
Tanshi’s feet were white; Luocha’s eyes were blue. Senghong cast statues;
Shi Xing burned scriptures. Daorong was the foremost among those who attained realization; Zhaoguan was the first in wisdom. Zhishun upheld the precepts; Daofang received the Vinaya.
Daocao [practiced]... Mingche [practiced]... Daoying lay upon the ice; Huiman sat amidst the snow.
Zangmu swallowed the stars; Xuanqin dreamed of the moon. Hui Long was as cold as the pines; Lang Gong was as pure as frost.
Daochang held fast to his resolve; Wangming maintained his integrity. Sengke had his arm severed; Fayuan had his teeth broken.
Yuandu flourished in the West; Jijin advanced in the North and East. Mitian’s eloquence was like a cauldron; Fa’an obtained the bell.

(The original text had no title. I have now provided one for the sake of researchers, following the precedent of other *Mongqiu* (Elementary Learning) works. Where the original was damaged by insects, I have supplemented it from other extant versions of the biography. To distinguish these supplementary passages from the original text, they are written in smaller characters.)

Regarding doubtful or erroneous characters in the Yuan edition, annotations are provided at the end of each respective section. Furthermore, where the Yuan edition was collated against alternative versions, these were noted in the margins of the main text; now, all such doubtful or erroneous readings have been standardized according to the critical edition and annotated at the end of each section.

This book contains two hundred and fourteen lines and employs thirty-two rhymes. For the sake of easy reference, these are now marked above the grids. Furthermore, for those lines that employ *yue-yun* (assonance), their fanqie transcriptions are annotated beneath the lines.
The *Śākya-móngqiu* (An Introduction to the Śākya Teachings), Title Complete.
*Śākya-móngqiu* (with Preface). Volume One.
Composed by the *śramaṇa* specializing in the study of the teachings, Língcāo, of Zhèshuǐ.
I have indeed examined three editions of Huijiao’s *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), totaling eighty fascicles.

As I perused the texts and observed the events therein—the differences between the ancients and the present, and the traces left by sages and worthies—it would not have been possible to achieve this without the talent of the Duke of Zhou or the pen of Dong Fu.
Nevertheless, the meanings and principles are vast and manifold, and the scrolls are extensive and wide; having read them...
Those who study this may lack powerful memory and be prone to forgetfulness; for this reason, I have gathered its categories of events and investigated its extraordinary occurrences.
I have composed it with parallelism as its literary style and prosodic laws as its rhyme. It is titled *The Mêngqiu of the Śākya School*.

May future generations of children and youths recite it to clarify its words and investigate its principles, so that they may contemplate following in the footsteps of the ancient worthies and serve as the foundation for the five teachings.
This is the preface written on the full moon day of the fourth month in the year Jǐyǒu.
(Yú) Mātanga entered the Han; Senghui came to Wù. Mātanga was originally a native of Central India.

He converted those various kingdoms and manifested many miraculous responses. Initially, together with Zhú Fǎ... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the extant portion.)
When Lan was about to enter the territory of Han, he moved Emperor Ming to have a dream one night in which a golden man flew through the air and arrived.

The following morning, the Emperor assembled his ministers in great numbers to interpret the dream. The learned official Fu Yi said, "Your servant has heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions whose name is Buddha;
what Your Majesty dreamed must surely be him. Upon hearing this, the Emperor was greatly pleased and immediately dispatched the Langzhong Cai...
Dr. Cai Yin, Qin Jing, and others were dispatched as envoys to India to seek out the Buddha-dharma.

While on their journey, they encountered the two monks Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who were traveling toward them carrying scriptures and images; they subsequently returned together to Luoyang. Emperor Ming received them with profound courtesy and honor.
It was from the arrival of Mātanga that the teachings flourished extensively throughout the eastern lands.
Kang Senghui was a native of the kingdom of Kangju. In the tenth year of the Chiku era, he arrived at Jianye, where he established images and began to propagate his teachings.

At that time, as the state of Wu had never before seen śramaṇas, they were suspected of practicing heterodox deceptions. An official submitted a memorial stating: "There is a man from the Hu lands who has entered our borders claiming to be a śramaṇa;
his appearance and attire are extraordinary, and he ought to be investigated. The sovereign, Sun Quan, summoned Senghui to interrogate him.
He asked, "What miraculous responses have occurred? Hui replied, "Since the Tathāgata passed away, more than a thousand years have suddenly elapsed.

His remaining bones and *śarīra* relics manifest divine radiance without limit. In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stupas; the establishment of these towers and temples serves to manifest his enduring legacy.
Quan said, "If you can obtain a *śarīra*, I shall have a stupa built for it. If it proves to be false, the state has established laws [for such matters]."
Zhang Hui requested a period of seven days. When no sign appeared by the fourteenth day, Sun Quan remarked, "This is merely deception," and intended to punish him.
Hui again requested another seven days, and Sun Quan granted this special request once more. On the seventh day, they suddenly heard a resonant *keng* sound from a bronze vessel.
Hui went to inspect it and indeed obtained a *śarīra*; he presented it to Sun Quan, and the entire court assembled to behold it.
The light was of five colors. Sun Quan held the jar and poured its contents onto a bronze basin; the śarīra struck the basin, which immediately shattered.
He then forged it with fire and placed it upon an iron anvil to strike it; both the anvil and the hammer were dented, yet the śarīra remained undamaged.
Sun Quan rose in solemn awe, crying out in admiration and prostration. From this, the construction of stūpas and monasteries flourished.
Huìzé was like a stone jar; Bǎoyì was a bronze pitcher.
Huìzé was by nature extraordinary and excelled in eloquence. During the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, there was a widespread epidemic throughout the land.
Huìzé then prayed with sincere devotion day and night, vowing that the heavenly deities would descend with medicine to heal the myriad people. One day, as he emerged from the monastery, he saw two...
The stone was shaped like a jar and was suspected of being some extraordinary object. Upon taking it up, there was indeed divine water within;
those throughout the world who drank of it were all healed.
Baoyi was a person from India—what the Hu call Anamodi—who came to this land to practice dhyāna beneath a tree.

He lectured on the sutras and śāstras and was also skilled in divine mantras (dhāraṇīs). Emperor Shizu of the Song dynasty held him in high esteem and bestowed upon him a bronze spittoon about two chi in height, which he kept constantly before his bed.
One day, it was suddenly stolen. He then took a piece of sitting matting, rolled it up empty, and cast a mantra over it.
After three nights had passed, he saw the spittoon returned, resting upon the matting.
Sengchou was slandered and Huisi was falsely accused. As for Sengchou:

his character was pure and upright, and he was renowned for his filial piety and faith. He was summoned to serve as a University Doctor (Daxue Boshi). Later, he left the household life and practiced meditation extensively.
He resided at Yunmen Temple on Longshan, west of Ye. Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty issued an imperial decree inviting him to enter the capital.
The imperial court’s offerings and honors toward him were extraordinary. Later, because of certain matters, a man named Chou slandered him, claiming he was arrogant and disrespectful.

The Emperor became greatly incensed and came in person, intending to kill Chou. Chou knew of this in advance through his spiritual insight and said to the assembly, "Tomorrow a great guest will arrive;
prepare many offerings. At midnight, he first prepared a bullock cart and went alone to the valley mouth, twenty *li* from the monastery.
He stood alone by the side of the road in another village until dawn. As expected, the Emperor suddenly arrived. Seeing Sengchou, he asked him in astonishment why he was there.

Sengchou replied, "I feared that the blood from my body might be impure and defile the monastery; therefore, I have waited here for you. The Emperor dismounted, prostrated himself, and repented his transgression.
He said to Yang Zunyuan, the Chancellor of the Secretariat, "How could one slander such a True Man? Thereupon, he personally carried [Sengchou]...

Huida returned to Chousi Temple. Huida struck his *ghaṇṭā* and refused [the invitation]. The Emperor said, "I, your disciple, have brought shame upon you throughout the world; this is not enough to atone for my transgressions.

As for Huishi, he was compassionate and harmonious from childhood and attained sudden awakening to *dhyāna* and tranquility. During the Guangda era of the Chen dynasty, he arrived at Mount Nanyue and encountered one...
At a place of forest and springs, he said to the assembly, "In a previous life, I once resided here.

Following his words, they dug there and indeed discovered the foundations of chambers and pavilions, as well as monastic utensils. At that time, a follower of a heterodox path, harboring jealousy, secretly informed the Chen Emperor, falsely accusing Sengsi of destroying Mount Heng.
The Chen Emperor dispatched an official to the mountain to investigate; there he saw two tigers roaring furiously beside Sengsi.

[The bees] retreated in terror and fear from its side. Later, when it attempted to advance again, it was once more obstructed by the venomous bees. Before long, those who harbored malicious thoughts toward it died suddenly.
The Emperor of Chen then welcomed it back to the capital, where the entire court paid it ritual homage and provided offerings.
Faxi painted a horse; Baozhi painted a crow. Faxi was a native of Nanhai.

His appearance was ugly and his spiritual anomalies were unfathomable. He resided in the region beyond the ridges (Lingbiao). According to the oral tradition of the elders, they had seen him since his childhood;
it is said that Faxi was approximately three hundred years old. During the Chen dynasty, Ma Jing served as the Governor of Guangzhou.
When the Provincial Governor (Cishi) was about to take office, he joyfully ascended the hall and drew a horse’s head on the ground with his finger to demonstrate [his intent].

Jing possessed great military strategy, and thus he governed the commandery. Whenever he traveled through the provinces, he led tens of thousands of armored soldiers, often manifesting a formidable and awe-inspiring presence.
The people reported this to Emperor Chen, who immediately dispatched the Marquis of Linru to observe the situation.
He remarked that there must be signs of rebellion, so he captured and executed him. The prophecy concerning Maitou was fulfilled within a month.
Baoshi initially resided at Daolin Temple to cultivate the teachings. He constantly carried a single *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), with a sky-illuminating pair of scissors hanging from its tip.

As he traveled to convert others during that time, he manifested many miraculous wonders. When Yin Qizhi, the Marshal of the Grand Commandant under the Qi dynasty, was accompanying Chen Xian-da in his campaign to garrison Jiangzhou, he took leave of Baoshi.
Baoshi drew a crow upon a piece of paper perched on a tree and said, "Hurry!"
At that time, he was able to ascend this [mountain]. Later, when Qizhi rebelled against the dynasty, he remained at the garrison of Zhizhou in the Qi state.
When he was defeated, Qizhi fled into Mount Lu. As the pursuing cavalry were about to overtake him, Qizhi saw a crow perched on a tree;
the crow did not leave at all. The pursuers, believing there was no one there, allowed him to escape. That crow and its tree were exactly as depicted in the illustration by Zhì.
**Sengyu’s Twin Paulownia Trees** Shao Shuo’s Single Sandal: Sengyu entered the gates of the Śākya at a young age and vowed to perform self-immolation by fire.

During the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he gathered wood to construct a funerary chamber, invited monks to a vegetarian feast for his final parting, and then entered the flames. After three days had passed, twin *tóng* trees suddenly sprang up inside Sengyu’s room. **Sengyu’s Twin Paulownia Trees** Shao Shuo’s Single Sandal: Sengyu entered the gates of the Śākya at a young age and vowed to perform self-immolation by fire.

During the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he gathered wood to construct a funerary chamber, invited monks to a vegetarian feast for his final parting, and then entered the flames. After three days had passed, twin *tóng* trees suddenly sprang up inside Sengyu’s room.

The roots and branches grew lush and abundant, their verdant foliage surpassing the ordinary until they eventually formed a "joined-heart" tree (*lianli*). Monastics and laypeople alike marveled at this, calling him the "Monk of the Twin Tō Trees.
As for Shao Shuo, he was a native of Shichang; he entered and left [the monastery] regardless of whether it was day or night. His secular surname was Shao, and after entering the Way...
He called himself Master Shuo. His speech and jests with others were all filled with symbolic prophecies (*fu* and *chen*). Later, he died at Mingshan Temple.
As he was about to pass away, he said to the practitioner Fajin, "You may leave my remains exposed on the road; however, quickly tie your sandals onto your feet.
Subsequently, they followed his instructions and placed the corpse outside the temple. After three days had passed, it suddenly vanished. Shortly thereafter, someone arrived from Pei County.
When [Zhao] Lü came, he encountered Jin, who said, "Yesterday I saw Master Shuo in the marketplace with one shoe on his foot.
He said, 'Young man, you must not go about like this; you have lost one of my shoes. Jin was startled and said, "The lacing on Master Shuo's foot was too tight, while the right foot was too loose;
it was because of this that the loss occurred. (The character "yún" [said] in this passage should be "yuè" [exclaimed]. "Yù Jìn" should likely be "Guò Jìn.")
Huiman extinguished the fire by planting *xiāng* (saliva) in the water.

Huiman was profoundly versed in the Sūtras and Vinaya and composed many commentaries and sub-commentaries. Once, while traveling to spread the Dharma in Fucheng, he was temporarily residing in a detached courtyard of the Wei Bingcao’s residence, where he was lecturing on the *Karmavācanā*.
Suddenly, the thatched hall where he lived was engulfed in flames; wind and fire raged together.
When it was full, Daosheng summoned some water and sprayed it [upon the vessel], whereupon it immediately ceased.
Zhi’s conduct was pure and austere, and all held him in high esteem. While residing in Baxi, he propagated the teachings of the Dharma.
As he traveled along the banks of the Hengnong River, he saw someone fishing; he exhorted him to desist, but the man would not follow his words. Daosheng then spat into the water, and suddenly—
A large snake raised its head and came toward him. Startled, the fisherman repented his error and immediately went to Sengxiang to leave the household life.
He respectfully took up the pen [to record his vow]. Jia Yi presented paper to Jingtuo.

He was profoundly versed in the meaning of the scriptures and possessed great dignity and exemplary conduct; at that time, people collectively regarded him as the preeminent figure among the monks. (Sui Dynasty).
The Emperor summoned him into the inner palace to lecture on the various sutras. He was granted a large bamboo fan over three feet wide, which he was ordered to carry with him.
Whenever he entered or left the palace, the Emperor would sometimes watch him from afar, remarking, "Truly, he is a preeminent monk.
When he was constantly engaged in his studies, he would often carry his own burden, placing his mother on one end and his writing brushes and scriptures on the other. At mealtimes, he would leave...
His mother would enter the village to beg for food beneath a tree. His writing brush handle was as large as an arm and three feet long.
When someone requested a calligraphic work, he would lay out a large sheet of paper and write but a single character; yet if they desired more, it would follow the brush and be completed.
It was never refined or adorned with artistic flourish, yet its spiritual wonder was such that onlookers never grew weary of it.
Jia Yi. It is unknown who he was. At the beginning of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, he came to Anlu. All his words were accompanied by spiritual manifestations.
Later, people saw him simultaneously in various places; only then did they realize he had manifested multiple bodies.
At that time, the Dharma Master Huigao of Fangdeng Temple saw Yi, who presented Gao with fifty sheets of paper, saying, "The Dharma Master shall attain understanding through this. Gao—

Later, he was imprisoned on account of official business and interrogated; when asked for a written statement, he replied that his paper had run out. When the matter concluded, he was released and spared. Thus his words were indeed fulfilled.
Mingdu called out for a dove, and Seng’an summoned a pheasant.

Fahu (Dharmarakṣa) was devoted to the recitation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. He resided at Shibisi Temple in Bingzhou. At that time, there was a dove’s nest on the eaves of the building, and the doves were rearing two fledglings.
Fahu would regularly bring them rice gruel and food to the nest to feed them, saying, "By the power of my recitation of the sūtras, may you grow up quickly.
Suddenly, the doves flew away and fell to the ground, both perishing. More than ten days later, he dreamed of two young children who said, "We are..."
"These two pigeons have, by virtue of the power of the Superior’s scriptures, been reborn among humans as the sons of a certain family ten *li* to the east of the monastery.
Dao went to that family to inquire, and indeed there were twin sons. Dao entered and called out, "Pigeon children!

whereupon they both turned their heads at once and responded in unison. After more than a year, they were able to speak. (As noted in the marginalia of the original manuscript: "One version reads 'human bodies,' which is acceptable.")
The monk An was of unknown origin. During the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty, he gathered disciples at Mount Wangwu to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
When he first began the title of the discourse, a female pheasant came before his seat and crouched down to listen. Whenever the monk went outside to eat or drink, the bird would follow him out.

Once the lectures on the three fascicles were completed, the assembly all marveled that she had not returned. An said, "The pheasant has now been born into the human realm; there is no need for wonder. [End of entry] Wu...
Hui-an led his disciples to Yue. Suddenly, he remembered that a hen pheasant from years past must have been born there. As they passed a house, he called out for the "hen pheasant" from afar.
A young woman came running out as if recognizing him from long ago. The family was astonished and marveled; they led An inside and prepared a meal for him.
An asked, "For what reason is she named 'Hen Pheasant'? They replied, "When we first saw her being born, her hair was like the tail feathers of a pheasant. Once [the story was told]...
"It is so. Because she was a female, she was named 'Cock Hen' (Chizi). An then recounted the original circumstances:

Formerly, the two sages of the Northern Mountains and the seven worthies of Western India—Fadu and Fashao of the Wei dynasty—traveled and studied in the northern lands, thoroughly mastering the Tripitaka. Their spiritual traces and extraordinary deeds were witnessed by all the world."
I have heard that at that time he resided at Xiqia Temple on Mount Nie; thus, he was popularly known as one of the "Two Sages of the Northern Mountains.
During the Jin dynasty, there were seven monks from Western India who were equally proficient in both Confucianism and Buddhism, engaging in timely debates.

Consequently, Sun Chuo composed the *Taoxian Lun* (Treatise on the Worthies of the Way), wherein he compared these seven Indian worthies to the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove, matching Dharmarakṣa with Shan Juyuan. Dharmarakṣa...
Zu Faji was compared to Xi Kang; Zhu Qian to Liu Bo-lun; Yu Falan to Ruan Sizong; Zhu Facheng to Wang Jun-chong;

Yu Daosui to Ruan Xian; and Zhi Dun to Xiang Ziqi. These seven worthies were thus paired with the seven monks, all based on an examination of their character and spirit, a comparison of their realization of the Way, and an assessment of their virtues. This treatise on their writings became widely circulated.
At that time, Fachong entered meditative absorption while Huikuan sat in dhyāna.
Fachong had left home at the age of eight; his spiritual conduct was preeminent, and he took meditative concentration as his path. Initially, he arrived at Xiangyang under the *san* tree.

He established a chamber for the practice of meditative concentration on Mount Gai. When the Prince of Jin’an of the Liang dynasty came to the region of Xiang and Yong, he heard of Sengcong’s reputation and consequently built a meditation hall for him.
Thereupon, he saw a fierce fire blazing; after a long while, it suddenly transformed into water. Once the water subsided and vanished, the chamber reappeared.
Upon inquiring into the details of the matter, it was discovered that he had entered the meditative absorption of water and fire.

Residing near the White Horse Spring (Baima Quan), he took a white tortoise from within the spring and, holding it in his palm, said to the King, "This is a male dragon. He then likewise took a five-colored carp from the water and held it in his hand.
He further said, "This is a female dragon. The king and his retinue were struck with wonder and reported this to the High Ancestor [Emperor Wu].
Huìkuān’s surname was Yang. His parents had originally revered the Daoist teachings and did not believe in the Buddhist school;

thus, they first gave birth to a daughter named Xìnxiàng, and later gave birth to a son named Huìkuān. He shared a deep affinity with his elder sister Xìnxiàng for secluded and tranquil places. At the age of...
At the age of five, he sat in meditation with Xinxiang in a quiet place. His parents, finding this strange, questioned him.
He replied, "The Buddha has come and taught me dharma gates such as the Prajñā, the Noble Wisdom Realm, and the Entrances. He then discussed these Buddhist teachings with his sister.

Their father followed a heterodox path and did not understand their words; however, by recording what they said, he obtained over two hundred sheets of paper. At that time, there was Master Huihui of Longhuai Monastery.

Upon hearing this, she went to see him. Her father showed her the text, and as soon as she opened it, she sighed in admiration, saying, "These words are entirely in accord with the principles of the Buddha.

Consequently, she and her sister left the household life to propagate the Dharma teachings widely. Her sister was held in high esteem by the King of Shu; people of the time called her the "Holy Nun" (Shengni).
Therefore, a temple was established for her, and she was also titled "Holy Nun.
Regarding Mingzan’s turning of stones and Luojie’s treading upon the spring:
Mingzan traveled to Mount Song and resided there for a long time. He propagated the methods of Chan meditation extensively, yet his temperament remained silent and unassuming. Later—
There was a Regional Inspector who, having received an imperial decree to sacrifice at the mountain peak, first had the road repaired so that it led straight to the summit.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, there was wind and thunder, and one peak collapsed. The mountain path below was blocked by a massive boulder.
He then tethered ten oxen to pull it away, and over a thousand men joined in with a clamor to push it; yet their strength was exhausted while the stone became even more firmly lodged.
Gu said, "Why do we need so many people? I will go with him. The crowd laughed loudly. Zàn then stepped upon the stone and moved it;
suddenly the disk turned and descended with a sound like a thunderclap. The governor, both clergy and laity alike, sighed in admiration, saying, "This is a great sage!
(The original biography reads "startled" instead of "laughed.")
Hālaka recited two million words [of scripture]. Later, he entered a stone chamber on Mount Luozhi to practice *dhyāna*.
Since this chamber was far from water, a lay devotee wished to open a mountain stream for him. Hālaka said, "There is no need to trouble yourself.
He then emerged from his meditative absorption and pressed his left foot against the western stone wall of the chamber; as his foot sank into the rock, a spring gushed forth from within. Its flavor—
Fragrant and pure; those who drink it receive joy.
Sengyou compiled the *Wanfa Jian* (Ten Thousand Dharmas Collection). Sengyou recited for a thousand monks.
From his youth, he entered the Śākya gate, specializing in the Vinaya-piṭaka and strictly adhering to ritual protocols. He resided in Jianye, where he gave public lectures.
The Vinaya School (Lüzong) constantly had more than ten thousand disciples who transmitted and upheld its teachings.
Fabian, since entering the Path, had always diligently practiced recitation and study. He resided at Wuceng Temple in Yizhou, serving as an attendant to Gui, the younger brother of Prince Wuling.
When the Wei dispatched General Wuti Hui to invade, Gui surrendered; within the city...
Both the monks and the Daoists were placed under confinement. At night, a brilliant light suddenly appeared. Huijing followed the light to its source and saw that all the other monks were asleep;
only Sengjian sat upright reciting a sutra, with light radiating from his mouth. Huijing then asked Jian what sutra he was reciting.
He replied, "I am reciting the lower fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Huijing said, "Why do you not recite it from the beginning? He replied:
When he had recited up to this point, Senghui asked, "How much have you been able to recite, Dharma Master?
He replied, "I resolved my mind to recite one entire *piṭaka*, but thus far I have only managed to recite one thousand fascicles. Senghui was struck with amazement and could not believe it;

wishing to test him, he requested that he recite it once through, asking, "Would it be too much trouble? Huijian said, "Reciting the sutras is my constant practice. Thereupon, a seat was prepared and he was invited to recite the sutra for seven days and seven nights.
The sounds of the night did not cease for even a moment.
Shi Zong leaned against the embankment, while Beidu carried a basket on his back.
Shi Zong was of unknown origin; he always wore a hempen robe, and the world called him the "Hemp-Robed Immortal. He resided in Bai... at Guangling.
He relied on earthen embankments to sing and chant for his own pleasure. Whether in seclusion or in public, his tracks were never fixed.

Once, while merchants were traveling by sea, they encountered a śramaṇa on a solitary island who entrusted a letter to Huizong. The letter remained inside the ship; though the merchants wished to see it, it would not detach from the vessel.
When they reached the White Earth Embankment (Baitudai), the letter flew up of its own accord and settled into Huizong’s palm. (From the *Taoxuan lüeshu*)
The *Miscellaneous Biographies of Yuanming* states that there were two extraordinary Dharma masters at Baitu Dai, and Zong was one of them.
As for Beidu, his name and origin are unknown; he constantly crossed waters by riding upon a wooden bowl, and his divine powers could not be fathomed.

He wore a rope belt and tattered robes that barely covered his body. His speech was inconsistent: at times he would bathe in ice-cold water, and at other times he would wear wooden clogs while climbing mountains.
Carrying nothing but a single reed ring, he traveled toward Guangling. He encountered a family at a village house observing the eight precepts;
though they had no prior acquaintance with him, he went straight to them and sat down, placing his ring in the courtyard.
When the family saw his appearance was so humble and wretched, they failed to show him due respect. Desiring to move the ring, they tried to lift it but could not; they then summoned ten men.
When they tried to lift it up, it would not budge. Looking further into its interior, they saw four small children, each several inches tall, with dignified and handsome features.
The family was immediately struck with great alarm.
Shengshi’s beard grew out, and Li Gong’s teeth remained whole.
During the Northern Wei dynasty, there was a Meditation Master named Sheng; his given name is unknown. From birth, he recounted the events of his previous life.
His parents, fearing he would leave the household life, pressured him into marriage, but he remained firm in his resolve without wavering. Upon entering the capital, he was ordered to be castrated.

The official, however, submitted a memorial requesting that he enter the mountains to alter his appearance and cultivate the Way. He was granted a copy of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which he recited day and night;
after more than a month, his beard and whiskers grew back.
Fali was born with a full set of teeth, which were firm, white, and brilliant; they remained so until his death, never decaying or falling out.

Since entering the Way, he had profoundly mastered the Great Teachings; his fame spread throughout the four seas, and both monastics and laypeople looked up to him. Indeed, he possessed qualities that were extraordinary compared to ordinary men.
Yǔguāng and Dàolǒng followed two distinct paths; Nénɡxiù were the two patriarchs.
In the city of Yè during the Wèi dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati instructed Huìguāng. Huìguāng led his disciples and transmitted his teachings in the region south of the capital.
The Tripiṭaka Master Bodhidatta instructed Dàolǒng. Dàolǒng led his disciples and transmitted his teachings in the region north of the capital.

In the north, there were two great routes at the former site of Ye, which were highly renowned at the time. Furthermore, the doctrines of the "Four Schools" and "Five Schools" originated from this region.
Huineng resided at Shuangfeng on Caoxi, while Shenxiu dwelt at Mount Dangyang in Jiangling; both transmitted the Dharma.
The method of *mo* flourished throughout the world, with practitioners vying for preeminence in their virtuous conduct. Consequently, the teaching spread to both the north and the south;

because of his capability, Huineng was established as the Southern School, and because of his excellence, Shenxiu was established as the Northern School. From this point on, the designation of these two schools became widely renowned.
Xingxin wept for his ox; Tanyou knocked on the tiger’s door.
As soon as Xingxin was born, he delighted in scriptures and images, as if already knowing the Way of the Empty Gate (Śūnyatā). His parents therefore allowed him to leave the household life.
At that time, he was four years old. On the road, he saw an ox-cart stuck in the mud, unable to pull itself free despite its efforts. He wept incessantly with grief.
When people asked him the reason, he said, "I pity its exhaustion and suffering so great."
Tanyou, having cultivated the path of dhyāna, lived in seclusion at Mount Shicheng in Shangshan. Later, he moved to a stone grotto on Mount Chicheng to practice seated meditation.
There were always several dozen tigers crouching before him. While Tanyou was reciting the sutras, one of the tigers fell into a deep sleep.
Tanyou then struck the tiger’s head with his bamboo *ruyi* (ceremonial whisk) and said, "Why do you not listen to the sutras? Thereupon—
"Everyone listen. After a short while, several snakes emerged, each as large as ten arm-spans in circumference; they came together to hear the Dharma and then departed.
Huishchi of Longmen and Zhu Qian of Ponghu: Huishchi was the younger brother of Huiyuan.
His character was refined and elegant, and he excelled both in doctrinal understanding and spiritual practice. He also served under Dao’an.
He became a master and resided together with Huiyuan on Mount Lu. Leading more than three thousand disciples, Sengchi was at their head.
At that time, Fan Ning, the Governor of Yuzhang, invited Sengchi to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Abhidharma*. Scholars gathered there in great numbers.
Wang Xun wrote a letter to Fan Ning asking, "Between Master Huiyuan and Master Sengchi, who is the superior? Fan Ning replied, "Truly, they are both worthy elder brothers."
He was the younger brother [of Kumārajīva]. When Saṃghabhūti arrived at the capital of Shu, he widely propagated the teachings of the Dharma.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Huìyán and Sēnggōng, both of whom had previously resided in Shu; they were both renowned for their talent and were the preeminent heroes of the age.
Upon Saṃghabhūti’s arrival, they all submitted out of respect for his reputation. Those who ascended his hall and entered his chamber were said to have "climbed the Dragon Gate."
Zhu Qian, courtesy name Fashen, possessed great talent and capacity. Emperor Ai of the Jin dynasty repeatedly invited him into the palace to lecture.

At that time, Sima Jianwen served as Chancellor and was a close friend of Qian. Once, while visiting Jianwen’s residence, he encountered Liu Tan of Peiguo, who mocked him, saying, "Why does a monk wander through crimson gates?
Qian replied, "You see them as crimson gates; I, a poor monk, see them as wild weeds."
Huier returned to Mount Yang in Shan and subsequently disappeared from view. At that time, Zhi Dun sent a messenger to request the purchase of the Small Ridge at Wozhou, adjacent to Mount Yang.
Huiquan replied, "If you wish to come, I shall grant it immediately; have you ever heard of Nao or You buying a mountain to live in seclusion?

Hōgyoku Shutsun: Master Setsu brought forth rain.
Hōgyoku’s conduct was lofty and extraordinary; he rarely engaged with worldly affairs, as if perceiving future events as if they were before his very eyes.
Every evening he would dwell alone in a single room. A neighboring monk frequently saw clouds of five different colors issue from Hōgyoku’s mouth, and people all went [to observe].
He gazed at them every evening in this manner.
Master Shi was a man from Western India who did not eat the five grains and could travel five hundred li in a single day. He came to Chang’an during the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian.
At that time, there was a drought, so Fu Jian requested him to perform a dragon-summoning rite; shortly thereafter, rain fell. Whenever there was a great drought, he was requested [to act].
"It shall certainly bring rain. However, after the year had passed, no rain fell. Fu Jian prayed for it again, but it did not come. He said to his great minister Zhu Tong:
"If Master Shi Yao were still alive, would I ever have to distress my heart over the drought so much? Is this man of the Way not a Great Sage?"
Tanzun wept for his master; Sramana Baomo transformed his mother.
Tanzun’s understanding and practice were lofty and profound; he had recited the sutras and shastras until he was thoroughly versed in them. He served Bao Guang as his teacher.

Initially, while lecturing in Qizhou, upon hearing that his teacher Bao Guang had passed away, he could not help but wail with great grief, throwing himself from his bed onto the ground. From his mouth—

Blood flowed [from his body]. His filial piety and righteousness were such as this. He then traveled to propagate the teachings in Qi, Chu, Jin, and Wei, where he was recognized by Prime Minister Wang Gong, who subsequently appointed him as the National Preceptor (Guotong).
Guṇavarman—translated as "Virtue Armor" (Gōngdé Kǎi)—was a man of great spiritual practice and wisdom that surpassed ordinary men.

He was originally of the Kṣatriya caste. His mother used to habitually eat wild meat, and he urged Varman to resolve this matter. Varman addressed his mother, saying, "Among all living beings, there is none that does not cherish life;
to take the life of another is not benevolent. His mother replied in anger, "Even if I should incur sin, I shall—"
Mātaṅga said, "I shall take your place. One day, while boiling oil, he poured it over his own finger and said to his mother, "I shall take your place and endure this pain.

His mother replied, "The pain resides in your body; how could I possibly take its place? Mātaṅga said, "If you cannot take the place of suffering even for what is before your eyes, how much less so for the three miserable realms?
Thereupon, his mother prostrated herself and repented her faults; she refrained from killing for the rest of her life and, because of this, came to have deep faith and respect for Mātaṅga.
Dharmakṣema (Tuo-le-qi-you), whose courtesy name was Daoliu (Dao-jiong;
the character for "liu" is pronounced like "ru" in the rhyme of "rui"), was a man from the Western Regions who came to Luoyang. No one could recognize him. One day, he said to the assembly:

Thereupon, they collectively established a temple and resided there. The temple was more than one hundred *lǐ* from the city of Luò. [The Master] would go every morning to the various temples in Luò for the midday meal.
In the evening, he would beg for a single bowl of oil and return to the temple to provide lamps and candles. It was by means of this that he sustained himself.
It was constant. There was a man who was an adept at walking who wished to follow Le to observe his pace; he ran but could not catch up.
Le ordered him to grasp the corner of his robe, and they heard only the sound of the wind rushing past; before they knew it, they had reached that monastery in an instant.
Daojiong served Daoyi as his teacher. When Daoyi was ill, he sent four monks from the same monastery to Henan to gather stalactites from Mount Huo.
They entered a cave and had to cross several wooden beams over water; three of them drowned, and their torches were extinguched.
With no way to proceed, Daojiong did nothing but recite the *Lotus Sūtra*. Suddenly, he saw a light like that of a firefly; though he pursued it, he could not catch it, yet it illuminated [his path].
The opening was clearly visible, and he was thus able to emerge from the cave.
(Zhi) Sengda’s hair turned white; Jueming had red whiskers.

Sengda of the pseudo-Wei dynasty was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular learning, and at that time everyone praised him. However, his character was rigid and he antagonized others, leading to his expulsion and residence in [exile].
Dachangsha Da became bald-headed at a young age; thus, he was popularly known as "White-Headed Da.

Buddhabhadra—translated into Chinese as Jueming (Awakened Clarity)—was raised within the Buddhist community from childhood, reciting several million words of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and possessing a comprehensive understanding of their doctrinal principles.
Kumārajīva served him as his teacher. He was profoundly versed in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and possessed a natural talent for discerning subtle nuances from a young age.
He had a beard; at that time he was called "Red-Bearded Vibhāṣā" (Jiàomíng—his *Biànzhǐ* [Biographical Record] reads Jiàomíng).
Regarding the Dharma Master Bǎoqióng, the Master of Profound Discourse:
Bǎoqióng entered the Gate of Emptiness immediately after his birth. Although he was very young, he attained a thorough mastery of the sutras and śāstras. At first...
Master Yun of Guangzhai Temple studied and practiced [the teachings]. Later, he moved to attend the lectures of Master Xian of Nanjian, who praised him with deep admiration.
When Yun reached the age of five, he was appointed as a Dharma Master; together with Master Xian, they further expounded and propagated the teachings.
Upon reaching adulthood, his height was eight chi, his back bore dragon-like markings, and he had thirty-nine teeth; such extraordinary features were not limited to these alone.
Shenhui was exceptionally brilliant and gifted from his youth, possessing extraordinary spiritual qualities. He profoundly mastered both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings.

He composed over forty volumes of commentaries, essays, inscriptions, and treatises. Consequently, the eminent scholars of the four seas had this proverb: "The Great Master Śākyamuni, Shenhui, has simultaneously grasped the Dharmadhātu and the Tārā."

Lingrun Observes a Wildfire: Zhikai’s Vow at the Pond Lingrun was a man of refined conduct who possessed profound knowledge of both the secular classics and the Buddhist teachings. Once, while traveling with several fellow students through the mountains, he encountered a wild fire spreading across the wilderness.

As the flames closed in from all four directions, the entire group fled in panic; yet Lingrun walked calmly as usual. Although the fire pressed close to his body, he looked back [at the blaze] with composure.
He addressed his fellow students, saying: "Outside the mind there is no fire; fire is truly one's own mind. To say that the fire flees of its own accord is to claim there is no way to escape it.
Yet when the fire reached him and moistened his body, it suddenly dispersed and vanished."
Zhikai’s surname was Feng. His father died early, and when he was six years old, he listened to Dharma Master Jizang lecture on the "Fire-House" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
At night, he told his mother: "The one who understands the 'Fire-House' in this scripture is none other than my own person. This is my fire-house; it is I who should burn it."
Since the man was not burned, it was clearly understood that there was no self [ātman]. Throughout the night until dawn, he went to the monastery and entered the monastic order.
His physical appearance was dark in color, so he was known at the time as Wukai (Black Kai). At the age of thirteen, he began lecturing on the sūtras and śāstras.

He did not let his side touch the mat, and he did not accept offerings of food, passing his days with empty abstinence. Suddenly, a pond surged forth behind the Buddha hall. Kai then made a vow, saying: "I shall drink only..."
The water in this pond surpasses that of this life.
Minggong ate a deer; Daofeng ate a bear.
Minggong, when formerly in the secular world, was a cavalryman under Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty. His physical strength was equal to that of one of his companions.

At that time, everyone was suspicious and jealous. The Emperor, wishing to eliminate them, prepared two bundles of cakes. Inside one cake he placed a set of raw deer antlers; inside the other, five *sheng* of salt.
He presented both to them to eat, and they finished them entirely. The one who ate the salt had his belly split open and died.
He respectfully ate the entire deer antler without any hindrance; because of this, he attained awakening and left the household life. He resided at Huishan Temple.
Once, he contended with Chao Hua Temple over land; the latter summoned more than a hundred unruly men to seize the autumn harvest of Huishan.
The crowd was filled with anxiety and sorrow. Senggong said, "Do not grieve. He then took up a large rock, about which thirty men could barely move.

Senggong alone lifted it and flung it far away as if it were a small clod of earth. His followers fled all at once. (The character *fù* is pronounced *biào*, being a simplified form of the character for leopard;

Daofeng was renowned in his time as one who had attained the Way. Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty held him in high esteem and respect.

The Emperor ordered wine and a steamed bear placed upon the palace hall and commanded Daofeng to ascend the hall to partake of the meal. Without offering any words of refusal or modesty, Daofeng ate to his heart's content. The Emperor laughed heartily and departed.
Later, he told his disciples, "Remove the items from the head of the bed and take away the bed. Upon doing so, they saw what had been there before.

Sengshi had double pupils, and Fashou had joined eyebrows.
Sengshi was born with double pupils in his eyes, from which light radiated outward. His mouth was encircled by black moles shaped like a tilted dipper.

He carried "phoenix eggs" beneath his armpits, and the seven parts of his body were all level. Everyone marveled at these signs; indeed, he subsequently entered the Buddhist teachings and attained profound insight into the nature of reality.
The edict of Emperor Wen, the Taizu of the Zhou dynasty, truly stated: "The Master has double pupils, a partial likeness to Yu Shun;
his back is humped, a resemblance to the Duke of Zhou. He may indeed be called a treasure of the age."
Dharmamitra—translated here as Fashou—was a native of Western India who came to the land of Han at the age of seven.

He possessed great integrity and was well-versed in various scriptures. From birth, his eyebrows were joined; his physical appearance was extraordinary, and for this reason, the people of this region called him the "Joined-Browed Chan Master.
(Regarding "came to" [laiyu], it is suspected that based on his original biography, it should perhaps be "came to travel" [laiyou].)
Huìqiān [obtained] white jade; Biànxiàng [obtained] purple *zhī* fungi.

While constructing a stūpa at Ānhé Temple in Hǎizhōu, during the process of excavating the ground, he suddenly encountered a piece of white jade over one chi in width, its radiance bright and brilliant. People...
Everyone marveled at this.

Bianxiang studied the sutras and treatises in his youth and was also well-versed in the Confucian tradition. When the imperial decree sent the śarīra relics to Dayu Monastery in Wuzhou, they suddenly emitted light of five colors.
At the site where the stupa was built, a branch of purple *lingzhi* fungus was found, over three feet in length, its luster and color extraordinary.

(Xian) Zhizang sat upon his seat; Dao’an ascended the carriage.
