As Huian was ascending the imperial throne, the ministers deliberated, saying, "The imperial throne is for the Son of Heaven alone to ascend; a śramaṇa must not be permitted to participate.

When Sengzang heard this, his expression suddenly grew fierce. He ascended the main hall, took his place upon the Dharma-seat, and said, "In my youth, when I was a lay official in the region of Wu, I felt no shame occupying the imperial couch;
how much less so now, as a disciple of the Buddha under the lineage of my ancestor, King Kāśyapa, the Golden-Wheel Monarch?"
"If you, patron, would kill me, then kill me; I have no concern that I shall have no place to be reborn. The Emperor then rescinded his decree, and Dao'an ascended the seat as before.
Dao'an’s character and conduct were lofty and brilliant, yet his physical appearance was coarse and dark. People of the time said of him, "The lacquer monk," and were struck with awe.

The neighboring state of Qin’s Fu Jian treated him with profound courtesy and respect. In a letter to various small states, Jian wrote: "When the Jin dynasty attacked Wu, their advantage lay in the two Lus.
Now that I have conquered Han, I have obtained but one and a half scholars. The Secretariat Director Quan Yi said: [This was the response].

"Who might they be? Jian asked. Huijian replied, "Master Dao’an alone, and Xie Zaochi as half a person. Later, when Jian went out to stroll in the Eastern Garden, he ordered Master Dao’an to ascend the carriage to ride with him.
Quan Yi remonstrated, saying, "I have heard that for the imperial carriage of the Son of Heaven, the Zhong-shi must accompany the occupant.
Master Dao’an has altered his physical appearance; he ought not to be included among them. Jian’s expression suddenly changed, and he said, "Master Dao’an..."
The Way has reached its ultimate realm, and his virtue is honored by the age. The weight of the entire empire cannot compare to it.
This is not a glory for you, my ministers, to have raised him; rather, it is my own distinction. Thereupon, I commanded Quan Yi to assist the Dharma Master in ascending the palanquin.
Fakai was talented and brilliant; Tanyan possessed quick wit and eloquence.
Fakai became renowned throughout the world for his skill in interpreting the meaning of the Dharma and his literary talent. He was a literary friend of Xie An, Wang Wendu, and others.
Thus, Sun Chuo characterized him, saying: "He deeply understood both the inner (Buddhist) and outer (secular) teachings; his talent was refined and his spirit transcendent. As for him...
As for Master Daokai, Emperor Ai of the Jin dynasty repeatedly requested him to lecture and expound the teachings.
Tanyan stood nine chi and five cun tall, with his hands reaching below his knees. He was profoundly learned in the Tripiṭaka and possessed extraordinary eloquence and discernment.

Because he held the ancestral rites of the Zhou in high esteem, he later entered the territory of Qin. At that time, there was a man from Chen named Zhou Hongzheng, who had profoundly mastered the teachings of Śākyamuni and was also well-versed in the Confucian tradition.
Possessing extraordinary eloquence, he traveled as a diplomat among the three kingdoms. During the Jiande era of the Zhou, he was commissioned to enter the territory of Qin.
Upon seeing his quick-witted eloquence, none of the great ministers at court dared to oppose him. The King of Qin then issued an edict throughout the realm...

Eminent debaters, regardless of whether they were monastics or laypeople, engaged in debate with Hóngzhèng. At that time, the Regional Inspector, Lord Zhōngshān of the Yùwén clan, submitted a memorial requesting his invitation to the capital.
The Prince of Qīn then convened a great assembly of the learned and capable to observe their debates. Hóngzhèng took the seat of honor.
The Ruler of Qīn asked, "Why do you not pay homage to the Triple Gem? Hóngzhèng replied, "My own strength is already meager; I do not rely on external support."
The holy and the wise provided him with their assistance. Consequently, he engaged in debate on the Three Teachings with Daorong.

Since Daorong was unable to respond to the many questions posed to him, and his eloquence failed to be swift, he descended from his seat, voiced his admiration and submission, and prostrated himself to take [Hui]yan as his teacher.
He attended upon him morning and evening, referring to him as "Bodhisattva Tanyan."
Daozheng emerged from the mundane world; his wisdom was praised for entering the Path of Goodness.
Daozheng’s secular surname was Zhao and his given name was Zheng; his courtesy name was Wenyue. During the Later Qin dynasty, he rose to the rank of Grand Governor of Wuwei.

By nature, he was fond of offering satirical admonitions. Toward the end of Fu Jian’s reign, when Jian favored the Xianbei people, Zheng saw both Jian and the Xianbei and then sang this song: [Song omitted as per instructions]
He said: "I have heard of old that the Mengjin River makes a single bend for a thousand li. This water was originally clear; who has stirred it to make it turbid?
Sengjian moved his expression and replied, "It is I. He spoke again: "In the northern garden there is a jujube tree; its leaves spread wide, casting a heavy shade."
Though thorns abound on the outside, within he truly harbors a heart of crimson sincerity. Jian said, "Is this not Zhao Wenyue?

It was precisely through this that he suddenly attained awakening to the teachings of Śākyamuni; he thereupon left the mundane world, changed his name to Daozheng, and traveled with the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta in Xiangyang, widely propagating the Dharma.
(The term "ji jian" should likely be read as "gui jian," meaning "to offer admonition.")
Zhicheng’s secular surname was Pei. From childhood, he naturally delighted in archery and horsemanship; at the age of seventeen, he became a military officer.

Later, while campaigning northward against the Xianyun, whenever he encountered combat, his heart was filled with compassion. He consequently sighed, saying, "To harm others for one's own salvation is not the will of benevolence.
He then cast off his armor, sought out a teacher, and entered the monastic life. Under the Venerable Master Nanjian Zong, he studied until he attained great understanding.
He mastered the various scriptures, and his fame resounded far and wide. Later, he gathered more than ten thousand students. At that time, a monk from Dengzhou—whose name is not recorded—came there;
he ate two pheasants daily. Both monastics and laypeople were indignant at this. (Note: "雉鳩" refers to pheasants;

"法朗" appears to be a transcription error for "法朗" [Fǎlǎng], though the context suggests a commoner's name or a misspelling; "猴犬" likely refers to the monk's behavior being as base as a monkey or a dog.)
It was unwholesome. At every meal, he set it aside as a dish. Later, a poor man came to beg for alms; the monk then divided two legs of the bird and gave them to him to eat together.
When the monk had finished eating, he ordered water for washing and rinsing his mouth. Suddenly, he saw the pheasant and the pigeon from before fly out from his mouth.
One was able to walk, while the other crawled on all fours on the ground. The poor man was greatly astonished;
unconsciously, he also produced two pheasants and doves, whose legs were fully formed. Monastics and laypeople marveled at this, calling him the Master of the Pheasant and Dove from Nanyang.
Falar entered the Way and resided in Ezhou. He ate and drank like ordinary people, which at the time was commonly criticized by others.
He kept a monkey and a dog that were large in stature; they accompanied Falar wherever he went or sat.

When it was time to eat, the monkey and the dog would bring wooden bowls to receive food and eat together with Falar. Once the meal was finished, the monkey would place the wooden bowl upon its head and ride atop the dog.
He traveled together with them on his back; his recitation was as clear as if he were chanting aloud, yet the monkey and dog lay prostrate listening.
His voice issued forth like thunder while his lips remained motionless; its spiritual wonder was unfathomable.
(Dao Rong’s *Qin* [Preface]: "When Dao Rong was young, he recited [the classics]; Zhi Xuan, when still a child, chanted the Way.
At the age of twelve, Dao Rong applied himself diligently to his studies. His teacher ordered him to read secular texts first, so he went to the village to borrow the *Lunyu*.
It was not until evening that he returned with the book; in fact, he had not borrowed it at all. Upon returning to his room, his teacher asked him the reason. He replied: 'He has already...'"
Upon finishing the recitation, the Master borrowed another copy to cross-check it; he did not omit a single character. The assembly was greatly astonished and marveled at him.
Later, he indeed mastered the Tripitaka thoroughly and his fame resounded throughout the world (the phrase "天下振名" likely means "his fame shook the world").

Zhi Xuan, whose courtesy name was Houjue, was surnamed Chen. Both his grandfather and father served in government office. Although Zhi Xuan was still in his swaddling clothes, he encountered Buddhist monks.
He was always filled with a look of joy. When he reached the age of five, his grandfather, seeing his intelligence and quick wit, had him recite a poem upon seeing flowers in bloom.
Within a few steps, he spontaneously composed this verse: "Flowers bloom, filling the trees with red; The flowers fall, leaving ten thousand branches empty."

Only one flower remained, destined to be carried away by the wind the following day. His grandfather sighed in astonishment, saying, "I had hoped this child would enter official service to bring glory to our family;
now I see his resolve is set upon entering the Gate of Emptiness. Not long after, he indeed requested ordination.
He mastered the sutras and śāstras with great proficiency, becoming a figure of extraordinary distinction whom people of the time widely praised.
Bian Gong: Cranes Descend; Sengfan: Geese Approach.
The monk Sengbian studied under the two masters Qian and Chang. He profoundly mastered the meaning of the scriptures and possessed a magnificent voice.
At that time, Liu Shao of Xinting invited him to recite the scriptural teachings. His voice was so pure and elegant that it moved a flock of cranes to fly down and settle in a row before him.
He listened until the scroll ended and then departed.

Sengfan of Dong in Yin, Qi, studied the Confucian tradition in his youth and later came to understand the Buddhist teachings. At that time, Du Bi, the Regional Inspector of Jiaozhou, invited him to lecture at Xianyi Temple.
Suddenly, a flock of wild geese flew down to the Dharma seat and sat listening. When the lecture concluded, they...
After he departed, a flock of sparrows was again moved to come before his seat and crouch down to listen. His spiritual wonders were manifold.
Pukang cut off his ears; Jing’ai severed his heart.
Pukang harbored a mind of diligent austerity and frequently dwelt in forests and wilds. Later, while staying at Zijing in Fanzhou, he stayed overnight in a cold forest.

When someone demanded his head, Sengkuang drew a knife and was about to cut it off when the beggar stopped him, saying, "I only ask for his ears. Sengkuang then sliced off both ears and gave them to him.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty, Buddhism flourished greatly, yet the followers of the Yellow Turbans (the Daoists) began to slander it. Sengkuang engaged them in debate;
when his arguments were proven sound and level-headed, he further sliced off one ear. Subsequently, he came to have no ears at all.

Jing’ai had lived in seclusion on Mount Taiyi since he first began studying the Way. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, having heard of Jing’ai’s reputation, issued an imperial decree to send a carriage and attendants to the mountain to welcome him, intending to appoint him to the rank of Senior Minister.

Jing’ai declined the offer and said to his disciples, "I see that the Great Dharma is falling into decline; I can no longer be of benefit to the teachings. I wish to sacrifice my body and life to repay the Buddha’s kindness."

The assembly all refused permission, and the students were filled with longing. Thereupon, [Hui]ai further compiled the *Sanbao ji* (Collection on the Three Jewels) in twenty fascicles and presented it to his disciples.
The Emperor again issued an edict urging him to comply, intending to go to the mountain himself. [Hui]ai secretly went to the top of a cliff and sat upon a flat rock.
He cut the flesh from his own body, laying it piece by piece upon the rocks; he drew out his intestines and hung them from the branches of a pine tree;

all the remaining muscles, flesh, hands, feet, head, and face were hacked into mincemeat and completely scattered. Only the bones and the heart-organ remained visible. He then cut out his heart, held it up in his hands, and passed away.

His disciples were struck with terror. (The character *yù* [轝] is pronounced *yù*; it is an earthenware vessel used for carrying. In the current text, this is likely a scribal error; it is suspected that the characters for "palanquin" (*luǎnyù*) should be used instead. Furthermore, the character *héng* [衡] is suspected of being a corruption of *wèi* [衛].)
Huiguo was digging for coins, while Huiyi was picking up gold.
Huiguo made the recitation of scriptures his primary task. Suddenly, he saw a ghost in the latrine who paid obeisance to him and said:

"In the past, I was a monk serving as a *karmadāna* (administrative official). Because I frequently acted contrary to the Dharma, I fell into this realm of ghosts that devour rice. Knowing that the Dharma Master is eminent and wise, I pray—"
To deliver him, he buried three thousand coins beneath the roots of a persimmon tree, intending for them to serve as a cause for merit.

Later, the ghost informed the assembly, who together dug up the site and recovered the three thousand coins. Having performed this good deed for the sake of the ghost, the ghost appeared again the following day and said, "I have already been delivered from suffering."
Huiyi had long studied the Buddha-vehicle and was profoundly versed in its great principles; he was held in high esteem by the Emperor of Song.

At that time, there was a practitioner named Facheng in Jizhou who, at the moment of his death, said to his disciple Puyan: "The spirit of Mount Song said, 'In Jiangdong there is a general Liu who shall receive the Mandate of Heaven.
I have used thirty-two jade disks and one ingot of gold as tokens of this. People [regarded] him as such."

When the matter was reported to the Emperor, the Emperor issued an edict to Yìyuè, saying: "This is an extraordinary matter. I wish to take [the relics], but it must be done by an extraordinary person.
Only then can they be obtained; if the Master does not go in person, I fear we shall not succeed.

Yìyuè then traveled to Mount Song, but though he searched, he found nothing. He then burned incense and offered prayers. On the seventh day, during the night, he dreamed of an old man with a long beard.
The old man took his staff and led Yi to the location of the jade discs, pointing and saying, "They are beneath this rock.
When morning came, Zhou traveled around the foot of the mountain until he reached a spot that resembled the place he had seen in his dream;
there, beneath the rock at the temple site, they indeed obtained thirty-two jade discs of various sizes and one ingot of gold. This matter was recorded in the *Song Shi*.
(Wei) Yuanxiao was difficult to oppose; Zhizhen was formidable.
Yuanxiao was a native of Silla who resided in that land. Because his understanding and practice were renowned for their brilliance, there were no local inhabitants who did not revere him.

He profoundly penetrated the Buddha-vehicle and extensively composed commentaries and treatises. At times he courageously challenged assemblies of scholars, and at other times he heroically deployed his literary arguments. He—
The ruler said to him, "Though there were ten thousand men, none could match your brilliance. Later, he entered China and greatly propagated the reputation of the Way.

Zhizhen, whose courtesy name was Huicheng, was intelligent and awakened from a young age and possessed great integrity. However, he was often severe and cautious. He had a profound understanding of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
While attending on Prince Xiu of Shu, he was invited to go to Faju Temple to assemble disciples and deliver lectures. There was a monk named Daohui who...
The man was fierce, savage, and exceptionally violent; seeing Sēn from afar, he fled to avoid him. The man asked, "You have never been afraid of a single person before;
why do you fear seeing Master Sēn? Huī replied, "This man is a king within the Buddha-dharma; how could I not fear him?
The man said, "Since you, Master Huī, are so brave, could you not match this one monk? Huī replied, "Even if my strength were equal..."
A thousand men saw Master Xun from afar; his pulses had already subsided and his four limbs could not be raised. What enemy could he have opposed?
At that time, they spoke among themselves, saying, "The Vinaya Master Xun is truly formidable."
Puming manifested his form; Hui Kan extended his arm to Puming.

Puming resided at Mount Tiantai, making the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) his primary task. Initially, he constructed a meditation hall that was narrow and small, and wishing to demolish it to enlarge it, he consulted with Master Zhiyi.
Zhiyi urged him not to alter it. At that time, there was Zhou Xiao, the Regional Inspector of Kuozhou.
Jie heard of this from afar. He provided cypress wood, which was sent across the sea. At that time, Ming was at Chicheng, and Zhiding was also there.
Suddenly, Zhiding saw Ming’s physical form standing ten zhang or more in height atop the cypress and pine trees, with a vast multitude of followers as his retinue.
When Xiaojie arrived, he and Zhiding witnessed it together; they were struck with wonder and marveled at his divine power.

Huìkǎn devoted his mind to the scriptural teachings and attained a profound mastery of their sources. He resided at Qīxiá Monastery. On one occasion, he came to the capital city of Yáng to visit Dharma Master Zīsī.

Zīsī had long been aware that Huìkǎn possessed miraculous powers beyond measure, so he requested that Huìkǎn demonstrate his spiritual might. Huìkǎn said, "If the Dharma Master grants permission, what difficulty could there be?
Huìkǎn then extended his arm through the window; it was over twenty *zhàng* in length. [He then] released [the beam] at Qíxī Monastery.
The inscription plaque from the Buddha hall was about to be brought back into the chamber. Huikuan said to Huikai, "People of the world lack far-reaching insight;

they are often startled and alarmed upon seeing this, which is why it does not manifest [to them]. You, Dharma Master, are brilliant and sagacious, so you dare to act in such a manner. (It was over twenty *zhang* long; the *Benzhuan* records it as several dozen *zhang*).
Xiaolong attained the Eight Penetrations (*aṣṭābhijñā*); Fazhou realized the Ten Wisdoms (*daśajñāna*).

Zhi Xiaolong of the Jin dynasty was well-versed in the various scriptures and also proficient in non-Buddhist classics. He shared a deep mutual understanding with Ruan Zhan and others, who regarded him as a true friend.

Because Xiaolong’s realization and insight were extraordinary, he was known at the time as one of the "Eight Sages" (Bada). At that time, a popular satire mocked Xiaolong, saying: "The Great Jin has risen like a dragon; the world is now our home.
Why does the śramaṇa not keep his hair and skin intact? Why does he not cast off the kāṣāya and discard the barbarian robes to don [Chinese dress]?"
[The Emperor presented] fine silks and brocades. The Dragon said: "To embrace the One is to roam in leisure; to abide in stillness is to achieve sincerity.

To shave one's hair, alter one's appearance, change one's robes, and transform one's form—others call this humiliation, but I cast aside their honor. Thus, by being without a mind for nobility, one becomes more noble;
by being without a mind for sufficiency, one becomes more sufficient."
Dharmatrāta was renowned for his literary talent and was also learned in the *Mūlamahāyānakarma-saṃgraha-sūtra*. He resided at Jingjue Temple in Quqi.

That temple was surrounded by lush, dense forests and featured winding, clear ponds, abounding in scenic beauty. Dharmatrāta then associated with ten people whose understanding and practice were in accord.
He studied both Confucianism and Buddhism here, composing verses on the wind and moon; at that time, he was known as one of the "Ten Wise Men of Quqi.
(Next: Scholar Huichao and Commandery Governor An Xuan.
Huichao entered the monastic order under Master Zhizang in his youth; he studied the sutras and śāstras until his understanding was brilliant and clear. He [was] among the students...
This was extraordinary. When Emperor Wu heard of this, he marveled at it and issued an edict appointing him as a Scholar of Shouguang Academy.
An Xuan had initially been a lay practitioner (upāsaka) and later became a monk. He had extensively mastered the Three Teachings, understanding them all without exception.

At the end of the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han, he traveled to Luoyang; by virtue of his merits, he was appointed as a Cavalry Commandant (Qi duwei). Gradually, he became proficient in the Chinese language and was able to propagate [the teachings].
Dianjiao lectured on the principles of the teachings with śramaṇas; he was what the world called the Commandant.
(Zhi) Zhiwen: "The peak of wisdom falls; the clouds of Dharma descend.
When Zhiwen's mother was pregnant, she dreamed of a Brahman monk holding a pine branch who said, "Henceforth you shall give birth to a son..."
[The Master] held a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) and thought, "It shall greatly propagate my teaching. After Wensheng passed away, [Huiguan] was exceptionally talented and stood out from the crowd;
he was thus ordained into the Way. Having mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka, he lectured on it day and night. He then dreamed that two dragons came floating across the sea.

When he opened a lecture at Dong'an Temple, as soon as he shook his fly-whisk, two mountain peaks suddenly collapsed. His disciples were astonished and marveled, and they went to inquire about the meaning of these signs.
Jianchu’s Dharma Master Qiong said, "This is an auspicious omen. There were two dragons that followed the Master as he preached the Dharma.
Among his disciples, there were very many; however, only Daozhi and Facheng succeeded to their teacher's Way."
Fayun’s mother was of the Wu clan. When Fayun was first born, she suddenly saw clouds filling the room, their radiance clear and translucent; for this reason, he was named Fayun (Dharma-Cloud).
After he left the household life, he did not change his name. At that time, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty held him in high esteem, regarding him as equal to Master Zhi.
Daoshi was also more eminent than Daoyun, who was titled Dalin Dharma Master. During one of Yun’s lectures, celestial flowers fell from the sky;
the entire assembly saw this and marveled at such an extraordinary occurrence.
(Hui-)cheng threw down his chopsticks; Dao-sheng picked up the spoon.
Hui-cheng was the courtesy name of Zhi-zhen. He was the younger brother of Master Xuan. At that time, Prince Xiu of Shu held a great assembly at Faju Temple for the sake of Zhen.
Suddenly, Zhen seized his chopsticks and asked Master Xuan, "Is this place maintained in ritual purity?"
Xuan said, "When I first returned, I had not yet conducted an inspection and learned that Dao did not maintain ritual purity.

Xun threw down his chopsticks and rose, saying, "I would rather eat the food of a butcher than consume this molten copper; how could it ever be eaten? At that time, more than five thousand monks in the assembly dispersed all at once.
Such was Master Xun’s strict adherence to and reverence for the Vinaya.
Zhu Daosheng was a disciple of Zhu Fatai. Initially residing on Mount Lu, he became renowned for his profound understanding as he lectured on the scriptures and teachings.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the Taizu, invited him to the capital and treated him with great honor, hosting a grand vegetarian feast for over ten thousand people.
The Emperor himself attended the assembly; when the crowd all doubted that it was too late for the meal to be served, the Emperor said, "It is just now."
[The monk] Zhong said, "The sun shines brightly in the sky; the sky speaks of 'beginning' and 'middle. How can this not be the middle?

Daosheng then took the spoon and sought food, immediately entering a fast. Thereupon, the great assembly followed his example. Such was his adherence to the mean (note: "chizhong" likely should be read as "zhèzhōng," meaning "compromise" or "synthesis").
(Geng) Wei Yan laughed heartily; Tan Ping possessed a powerful voice.
Huian, while still young, dwelt at Mount Yao in Langzhou to practice meditative contemplation. One night, under a bright moon, he ascended the summit of that mountain and let out a great laugh.
The sound echoed for more than ninety li to Liyang. That night, everyone in the households of eastern Liyang, both old and young, heard this great laughter and were all struck with wonder and alarm.
At dawn, they began inquiring of one another and investigating the matter until they reached [Huian].
The disciples of Yaoshan each said, "Last night, when the moon was bright, the Master ascended to the mountain peak and laughed loudly;
this must surely be it.

Tanying was skilled at chanting and exhortation; his voice was so powerful and grand that it could not be compared to anything else. When he uttered a single note, it was like an elephant [trumpeting].
The horses neighed mournfully, and they halted their journey on the road.
Regarding the two geniuses, Senghui and Mingyan (Ming is likely an error for Zhi; the original biography also reads thus), and the three sages: Senghui possessed brilliant talent from his youth.

He extensively composed commentaries on the meanings of the scriptures, and his eloquent expositions were versatile and profound. In his later years, he lectured extensively on the Tripitaka teachings.
Dian was a contemporary of Dharma Master Xuanchang, and both were renowned in their time; they were popularly known as the "Two Heroes in Black Robes.
Zhiyan was a high-ranking official of the court who renounced his glory to seek the life of a silent monk (*śramaṇa*) and vigorously propagated the teachings of the Dharma.

Zhiyan frequently associated with and frequented the company of Dharma Master Dao’an—the younger brother of the King of Linhai of the Chen dynasty—and the Tripiṭaka Master Bianzhi. The world [regarded them thus].

As for these three monks, their monastic conduct and wisdom were equal, and thus they were styled the "Three Eminences. Their fame spread throughout the four seas. Fatong (Dàofǎtōng) possessed great strength;
Daokai (Dàokāi) was vigorous in his practice;
and Fatong entered the Gate of Emptiness at a young age. He was extremely frail and weak, prostrating himself like grass before the wind. His companions looked down upon him, but Fatong shed tears.

He then made a vow before the image of Avalokiteśvara, saying: "May the Bodhisattva’s holy discernment take notice of me; I beg for your compassionate guidance so that I may be spared this humiliation.
Thereupon, he recited the mantra without ceasing. One day, returning to visit his aged mother, he dozed off while staying at his mother's house.
Suddenly, beneath a tree in the courtyard, he saw himself sleeping with three *sheng* of saliva and foam flowing from his mouth. His mother cried out in alarm, and he awoke.
A question was asked: "What event was such as this? Tong replied: "In a dream, someone sent me three donkeys laden with sinews and gave them to me.
I ate the sinews from one donkey; upon hearing a call, I awoke. From that time on, I possessed great strength in my tendons and muscles. People called me a sage.
At that time, there was a large stone mortar on South Mountain weighing over a hundred jin. Tong went and carried it back to Fahuai Temple in the capital. Later, he saw it again.
An ox-cart was harnessed and dragged along at full speed. At that time, the world’s strongmen marveled, saying he was a celestial athlete.
(The character "gu" [姑] in "gu yi lu" [姑一驢] is likely a scribal error for "ru" [茹]; alternatively, "gu yi lu" may carry the sense of "provisionally" [姑且].
Śrīmitra (Dānka) lived in seclusion in the mountain forests for his entire life, reciting over four hundred thousand words of scripture. While in the mountains, he subsisted solely on cypress wood.
[He] truly did so. Later, he consumed small pebbles. At that time, the Governor of Fuling sent a horse to meet Huidaokai;
K'ai declined the offer and traveled on foot for over three hundred *li*, arriving early the following day. Furthermore, during Jianwu of Shi Hu’s reign, he came from Xiping to Nan’an;
the road was over seven hundred *li* long, yet K’ai traveled it in a single day. He ordained a young boy as a novice monk.
Miyun was fourteen years old when he also inherited his master’s teachings; moreover, he was capable of traveling great distances and succeeded Kewen in the propagation of the Dharma.
Puhua carried a wooden staff, while Gong Huo dug a pit.
It is unknown where Puhua was from; he underwent a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, never adhering to any fixed pattern. At that time, he resided in Zhending Prefecture.
One day, Hui suddenly carried a coffin on his shoulder and walked through the streets, announcing: "I shall die tomorrow. No one could fathom this.
They followed him in a procession as he left through the eastern gate of the city, where he cried out: "Today’s burial is not in accord with the principles of the *Qingwu* (the art of geomancy).
Two days later, he went out through the southern gate of the city, and they followed him again. He said once more: "Tomorrow will be auspicious. When dawn broke the following morning, Hui then—
He sat alone in the wilds like one who had entered meditative absorption, and then he passed away.
Master Xiang arrived in Yizhou at Mount Qingcheng’s Feifu Temple during the early Liang dynasty.

At that time, it was the custom for people to go to the mountains on the evening of the third day of the third month to drink wine, eat meat, and gather medicinal herbs; Master Xiang exhorted them to cease this practice, but they did not stop. In the following year, on the third month again—
When they had arrived as before and were seated according to custom, Xiang ordered people to dig a pit about one *zhang* square beneath their seats; no one could fathom his intention.

Xiang said to them, "Lay patrons, you always eat and drink yourselves but have never given anything to me. Today, for the sake of the assembly, I must have a full meal. People vied with one another to offer delicacies and wine;
yet as soon as they were received, they were gone, as if filling a vast ravine. Those who understood marveled at this. It continued until evening.
He said, "I was so intoxicated and satiated that they helped me toward a pit. When I reached the pit, I opened my mouth and vomited profusely;
the chicken meat came out of my mouth and immediately flew away, the lamb meat came out of my mouth and immediately ran off, and even the fish, eels, geese, and ducks all remained alive.
The crowd was greatly startled and fled. I vowed to renounce wine and meat forever, and on this mountain, the practice of killing living beings was permanently abolished."
(Tang) Tanshi’s feet were white; Kumārajīva’s eyes were blue.
After Tanshi entered the Way, he performed many external acts of spiritual transformation while traveling and teaching in Guanzhong.

His feet were white compared to his face, and though he walked barefoot through mud and water, they were never stained. All under heaven called him the "White-Footed Monk" (Bai-zu Heshang). At that time, Helian Bobo...
While he was being executed in Guanzhong, Shi was subsequently killed; yet even when he encountered several blades in succession, none were able to harm him.

Thereupon, he went into hiding in the mountain forests. Later, when Tuoba Tao entered Guanzhong, Cui Hao of Boling—who harbored suspicions toward the Buddha-dharma—came to believe in the Celestial Master Kou Qianzhi.
Consequently, Tao and Hao proceeded to utterly extinguish the Buddha-dharma throughout the Great Wei in the seventh year of the Taiping era.
The soldiers burned and plundered the monasteries, and the monks and nuns were forced to abandon the Way. Those who attempted to flee were pursued; if captured, they were invariably decapitated.

When [the monk] first heard of this, he descended from the mountain and arrived at the palace gate with his staff. An official reported: "There is a man of the Way whose feet are whiter than his face, now standing at the palace gate.
Emperor Tuo ordered him to be executed, but the executioner could not harm him. He then reported this to Tuo. Tuo was greatly enraged and personally took up what he wore...

He struck it with his sword several times, yet it sustained no injury or damage whatsoever. At that time, tigers were being raised in the northern garden; when he first fed them, the tigers all remained hidden and did not approach.
When he tested them by approaching as the Heavenly Master, the tigers roared loudly and came toward him.

Knowing that the Buddha-dharma was exceptionally superior, Sui Hu withdrew, ascended the hall to pay homage and repent, and subsequently promoted the Buddha-dharma. (Regarding the phrase "entering Guanzhong," some editions include the character "again" [再]; regarding "diminishing the Buddha-dharma," some editions read "extinguishing the Buddhist teaching" [滅佛教].)

Vimalākṣa—translated here as "Undefiled Eye"—was revered by Kumārajīva as his teacher. Vimalākṣa was the first to specialize in the Vinaya Piṭaka and to investigate the origins of the precepts in detail.
Daochang’s Huiguan compiled a record summarizing the essential principles of the school's doctrinal judgments regarding the gravity of internal prohibitions;
this became widely practiced in the capital, with monks and nuns copying it out. At that time, the price of paper in Chang’an increased, and furthermore, the *Tian*... [text continues].
Lower: Furthermore, because his eyes were blue, people at the time all called him the "Blue-Eyed Vinaya Master.
Regarding Senghong casting an image and Shishang burning scriptures:
Senghong resided in the capital and cast a sixteen-foot golden image. Once the melting and casting were completed, before the mold had even been opened, at that time—

At the end of the Jin dynasty, the prohibition against casting bronze images was strictly enforced; those who violated it were all executed. Daohong was imprisoned in the Chancellor’s office and focused his mind solely on reciting the Buddha’s name.

During the night, he dreamed that a statue came to him and rubbed the crown of his head with its hand, saying, "Do not worry; you shall be released tomorrow. At dawn, he indeed heard that the execution was about to take place.
However, while the Governor’s Counselor supervised the slaughter, the ox bolted and the carriage overturned. Consequently, the date for the execution was set for another day.
Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict was issued granting him immunity from punishment.
After Zhu Shixing had left the household life, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of sūtras and śāstras until his understanding of their meanings became profoundly clear.

Later, he entered the shifting sands and reached the kingdom of Khotan, where he finally obtained the original Sanskrit texts of nine chapters of Mahāyāna sūtras. He then dispatched his disciples to carry them back to Luoyang.
At that time, the monks of Khotan all studied the Hīnayāna and were not versed in the Mahāyāna. They then addressed the King, saying:
"The śramaṇas from the land of Han wish to delude and confuse the True Dharma with the books of the Brahmins. Your Majesty is the lord of the land;

if you do not prohibit this, the land of Han will become deaf and blind, and the fault will lie with Your Majesty. The King immediately refused to allow the scriptures to be carried into Han. Shi Xing was deeply...
Carrying a heavy heart, he sought to burn Mahāyāna sūtras as proof. The King immediately granted him permission.

Thereupon, he piled wood before the palace and set fire to the scriptures. Kṣitigarbha (Shìxíng) made a vow, saying: "If the Great Dharma is destined for the land of Han, these scriptures shall not burn.
He then cast the scriptures into the flames; the fire was instantly extinguished without damaging a single character. He was thus able to take them back to Luoyang. This was the burning.

The events of the sutra took place at the end of the Han dynasty. This differs from the account of Dharmaratna and An Shigao during the time of Emperor Ming, when they competed with Dao Fa by burning scriptures.
(Zhì) was the foremost among [Seng]shēng and [Fashī]róng; [Seng]guān and [Huí]zhào were the first.
Song Daosheng and Daorong were both thoroughly versed in the principles of both Confucianism and Buddhism, their mastery of these doctrines being comprehensive and versatile.

Furthermore, Huiguan and Sengzhao also reached the depths of both internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist) learning, such that their dialectical skill was invincible. Thus, the eminent scholars of the time proclaimed: "In the depth of understanding, Daosheng and Daorong are preeminent;
in the precision of debate, Huiguan and Sengzhao are foremost. Their reputations spread far and wide.
Zhishun upheld the precepts. Daofang transmitted the Vinaya to Zhishun.
After entering the Way, he resided at Tuxian Temple on Mount Zhong. From his youth, he specialized in upholding the dharma of the precepts with extraordinary strictness.
He gathered disciples to chant [the scriptures], and those under him often numbered over a thousand. Later, he fell gravely ill. His disciple, Tan...
When Huijian saw that his master had been fasting for a long time, he secretly mixed a small amount of rice with honey, boiled it, and offered it to Huishun.
As soon as Huishun ate it, he vomited. He asked for water to rinse his mouth and said to his disciple Tanhe, "Leave the mountain gate at once;
you must not return here. You are no longer my disciple. Such was the strictness with which he maintained the precepts. (In the *Shanmen zhuan*, this is written as "Yunmen.")
Daofang was pure and upright in character and conduct. From his youth, he had mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka and diligently lectured and exhorted others, attracting many students.

He led them all to reform their evil ways; however, whenever there were those among them who did not change, Daofang would weep for them in sorrow and personally instruct them in the Vinaya scriptures.
Later, at the end of his life, he reached the age of one hundred and twenty, and everyone marveled at him.
Daochao [blank]... Mingche [blank] Daochao.

By nature, he was diligent and earnest from his youth, devoted to study. Though the dust of the inner and outer worlds covered him and the chirping of insects clamored in his ears, with dust burying his knees, he felt no resentment.
Daochao replied: "I hear the sounds of the insects at times; they are sufficient to serve as flutes and pipes. Although I guard against the dust..."
"I have not yet had the leisure to sweep. Such was the character of his rigorous training.
Mingche left home to become a monk at the age of six; he was renowned for his resolute will, steadfast integrity, and diligent asceticism.
Once, while he was with several fellow monks, the old foundation of their temple was decayed and collapsed under the force of wind and rain. With nothing to support it, the several monks all fled.
Sengche continued to live in his house and pursued his studies as before. When someone asked him, "The house has collapsed; why did you not flee?

Sengche replied, "Not even a moment’s time should be wasted. (The above text was destroyed by bookworms, leaving only these one hundred and nineteen characters remaining. Now, based on the extant fragments and the original biography, I have privately supplemented the meaning.
(The path transcends the dust-buried earth; the light pierces the severed beam.)

Daochao, surnamed Lu, was a native of Wu Commandery. From his youth, he was renowned for his diligence and devotion. Daochao lived alone in a separate room, isolating himself from visitors to focus on his studies. Dust and grime filled the interior of his chamber, and crickets chirped against the walls. Zhang Shuai, a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat, remarked to him, "The sound of insects is deafening to the ears, and dust covers your knees;

how can you remain unperturbed by such conditions? Daochao replied, "I hear the sound of the insects often enough; it serves as a substitute for flutes and pipes. Although the dust is thick, I have no leisure to sweep it away. Such was his fierce dedication to learning.

Mingche left home to become a monk at the age of six to study the teachings. He was renowned for his resolute character and diligent asceticism. He lived with several fellow monks in an old room belonging to his teacher; this room was originally dilapidated, and when wind and rain caused the roof to collapse, there was nothing to support it.
While the other monks all fled, Mingche remained in the room, continuing his studies as before. When someone asked him, "The house is collapsing; why do you not avoid it?
Mingche replied, "A moment of time is difficult to waste. Daoying lay upon the ice; Huiman sat amidst the snow.

Daoying took the practice of dhyāna as his vocation. His spiritual anomalies were reported repeatedly. Once, while traveling beside a pond in Longtai Marsh, he ordered his disciples to hold his robes;

he then stripped off his clothes and entered the water, remaining there for six nights before emerging. He declared, "Though I was in the water, it was only the dust from the worn-out earth that covered me.
Later, during a severe winter when the ice and snow were thick and heavy, he remarked, "This level ground..."
"I must not sleep," he thought, and so he stripped off his clothes and lay down upon the ice and snow. After three nights, he rose and said, "I nearly died from being scorched by fire.
Initially, when Huiman arrived in Xiangzhou, he met Chan Master Na, who transmitted the Dharma of Chan to him; through this, he attained great awakening.
He wore but a single robe and kept only two needles; he would discard them all during the summer and beg for replacements in the winter, having no other means of livelihood.
Later, while staying overnight among the cypress graves beside Huishan Temple in Luozhou, he encountered three feet of snow.
He then entered the temple and met the Dharma Master Tanguang. Tanguang asked him in surprise where he had come from. Faman replied, "I have come as a dharma-friend. Tanguang sent him away.
He searched around his seat and found that snow had accumulated over his body to a height of five or six feet. (The arrival of his Dharma friend is not specified.
[Moon] Zang’s mother swallowed a star; Xuanqin dreamed of the moon. Zhizang’s surname was Gu;
both his grandfather and father served at the Liang court. His father died early, and his mother resided in Wuzhong. Once...
She emerged and circumambulated the city of Wu once. Suddenly, she saw dense clouds spreading on all sides, yet the sky opened up and became clear in the center.

She saw various stars falling to the earth; she picked up one and swallowed it, and thereby became pregnant. When she gave birth to Zang, he was exceptionally intelligent and precocious. He left the household life and established the teachings.

Zhi Xuan, whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Meizhou. Both his grandfather and father held official posts. His mother, Lady Wei, became pregnant after dreaming that the moon entered her bosom; thus Zhi Xuan was born.
From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and attained a profound realization of the Buddhist school. He subsequently sought entry into the Way and later mastered all three Piṭakas.

He traveled to propagate the teachings throughout Min and Shu, where the people of Shu took refuge in his faith with such devotion that they could not bear to call him by his name, addressing him instead simply as "Chen Pusa" (Chen Bodhisattva).
Sāyán. (Xiè) Huìlóng’s pines were cold; Lǎnggōng’s frost was pure.
Huìlóng studied the Buddha-vehicle in his youth and attained a profound understanding of its principles. Emperor Míng of the Song dynasty invited Huìlóng to preach at Xiānggōng Temple.
He taught over one thousand disciples (the *Biographies* records eight hundred). Many of the eminent figures of the Song dynasty were his associates.
Yet, his integrity and appearance were like those of a pine in winter; thus, Zhou Yong of Runan remarked of him:
"Master Senglong is detached and austere, like a pine or bamboo standing beneath the frost. (The *Biographies* records "over one thousand" as "eight hundred.")

Huìlǎng was extensively learned in both Buddhist and secular texts and enjoyed a great reputation during the Liáng dynasty. He possessed a stout yet pure white complexion, appearing as if covered in snow and frost;
thus, a contemporary saying went: "Frost-pure and white Lǎng."
Daochang held fast to his resolve and maintained his integrity without seeking fame.
Daochang studied together with Daobiao; he possessed great talent and capacity, and was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka.

At that time, when Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, saw these two men, their spirit was brilliant and refined, and they possessed the capacity to govern a state. Thereupon, he ordered Yao Xian, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, [to oversee them].
He urged these two men to abandon the monastic path to assist in reviving the royal enterprise. Furthermore, he issued an edict to Chang and Biao, stating: "Your pure integrity is truly commendable.

However, as you preside over the four seas, the governance of the realm urgently requires talent. I wish to deprive you of your dharma robes so that you may assist in supporting and advising the state of the age.
If your hearts remain fixed on the flavor of the Way, what does it matter whether one is clad in white or black? I hope you will consider this intention."
They did not use their commitment to their vows as an excuse. Sengchang and the others each offered various responses, and so forth.

Daoxing again sent a letter to Kumārajīva and Sengrui, and the two masters sought to exempt these two men from abandoning the Way. Sengchang and the others were pressed incessantly, yet they remained steadfast in their resolve and could not be swayed.
He then threw himself into a rocky ravine and died. (According to Daochang’s biography, his name was Daoheng; "threw himself" is rendered as "escaped by throwing himself").
Wangming was a hereditary official of the gentry class who renounced glory to seek the Way. By nature he loved chanting and whistling, and he especially appreciated hills and forests.

His fame filled the world, and Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty treated him with great courtesy and respect. Upon meeting him, the Emperor perceived that his reputation, demeanor, and character were extraordinary, and that he possessed the talent for governing the state.
The Emperor consulted with his court officials regarding him, wishing to honor him with noble rank and emolument; however, he declined and did not accept. Mǔ maintained his integrity.
The Emperor remarked, "This is a man of lofty virtue and the Way," and subsequently composed the "Admonition on the Abandonment of Learning" (*Juéxué zhēn*), which circulated throughout the world.
Sengke had his arm severed; Fayan’s teeth were broken by Sengke.
Sengke took meditation as his primary task. When he first arrived, Bodhidharma began the transmission of the *Laṅkāvatāra* dharma to him.
Sengke practiced and studied amidst the forests and wilds; when he encountered bandits who hacked off his arm, he did not let anyone know and felt no sensation of pain.

Later, there was a man named Fa-lin who was also robbed by bandits and had his arm severed. He cried out throughout the entire night. Ke begged for food to provide for Lin’s medical treatment and bandaging.
Lin was surprised that Ke’s arm did not suffer any inconvenience and grew angry with him. Ke said, "I too have no arm; why does the Master wonder at this and grow angry?
Only then did the people of the world realize that Master Ke’s arm had been cut off.
Fayuan was a profound student of both Confucianism and Buddhism, whose reputation as a peerless master of the Way spread throughout Jiangxi.
His fame reached Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, who one day suddenly asked Fayuan why he ate only vegetables.

Fayuan replied, "Since I received the precepts, I have spent my days in a single fast, eating only vegetable rice. The Emperor persistently urged him to eat meat, but Fayuan remained steadfast in his resolve and would not waver.
Having no other recourse, he eventually broke two of his teeth to escape.
(East) Yuan and Du promoted [the Dharma] in the West; Ji and Hui promoted it in the East.

The monks Sengyuan and Tandu of the Song dynasty were both well-versed in the teachings of the Vehicle. Their exegesis of the principles followed one after another, and their Way flourished in Jiangxi.
People called them "Jewels.

Huìjī and Chāojìn were both distinguished by their excellence in practice and understanding; they were thoroughly proficient both internally and externally, and together they greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma in Jiangdong.
The people followed his transformation of them and revered him as if he were a deity.
(Winter) Miti Bianding, Fajian Huozhong, and Da'an.
When Xi Zuochi first visited Da'an, An asked, "Who are you? Zuochi replied, "I am a... [four characters].
Hai Xi asked Zao Chi, "I have already inquired after the Dharma Master’s well-being; what is his name? An replied, "Under the vast sky, there is Shi Dao’an.
From that time on, everyone called him "The One Who Covers the Sky" (Mitian). At that time, King Fu Jian of the Qin dynasty obtained a large bronze cauldron at Lantian that held thirty-seven *hu*.
There were seal-script characters on its sides, which no one in the court could decipher. He showed it to Dao’an, who said: "This..."
It was in ancient seal script and stated that it had been cast by Duke Xiang of Lu. Furthermore, he obtained a bronze *hu* (measuring vessel) in the market;

its shape was perfectly circular. The downward-facing part served as the *dou*; the horizontal beam, with its raised section (*miao*), served as the *sheng*, while the lowered section of the beam served as the *he*. One end of the vessel was the *yue*.
It was the same size as a *huángzhōng* vessel, with a capacity of half a *hé*. On its sides were inscriptions in seal script. Yao Xian again asked An about it.
An replied, "This was when Wang Mang declared himself a descendant of Emperor Shun. In the year *wùchén*, he reformed the calendar and ascended the throne.

He standardized weights and measures using the *tónglǜliàng* system and distributed them throughout the four quarters, desiring that vessels large and small be uniform so that the whole world might attain equilibrium. Yao Xian greatly praised him and issued an edict to the scholars of the Three Academies.

Whenever there were matters of doubt, they all consulted Master An. (The character "mǎo" [昴] should be "áng" [昂]. "Mǎo" is the name of an asterism; it is composed of "rì" [日] and "mǎo" [卯]. "Áng" means to ascend; it is composed of "rì" [日] and "yǎng" [卬]). Fǎ'ān was a disciple of Huìyuǎn.
He was dedicated to the study of the Sūtras and Vinaya, and he was particularly strict in maintaining his monastic discipline.
He resided in Xīnyáng County, where tigers were numerous. Fǎ'ān built a monastery there to provide safety for the local people. Later, wishing to have a portrait painted, he required...

He was distressed because he could not obtain the blue-green copper pigment (tongqing). One night, he dreamed of a divine being who pointed to the area before his bed and said, "Beneath this lies a bronze bell.
When he dug there the following morning, he indeed found two bells. He used one to complete the image, while the other was used to assist Master Yuan in casting an image.
Wu Chang, the Governor of Wuchang, borrowed it for inspection and kept it.
Chao Da hid himself in the grass. Nanda changed his staff;
this refers to Wei Chao Da. He was deeply learned and possessed great insight. At that time, Emperor Wu of the Wei dynasty prohibited the study of prophetic charts and texts with particular severity.
Someone falsely accused Da of possessing [prohibited items], and Da was consequently imprisoned. Cui Hao, the jailer of Yongyang, was ordered to investigate.

Da informed Hao of the truth, whereupon Hao became violently enraged. He had Da’s head bound to a wagon wheel and placed him under strict guard. Realizing there was no way out, Da focused his mind exclusively on Avalokiteśvara.
At night, he suddenly lost consciousness; those guarding the wheel were all overcome by deep sleep, and the prison gate—
Suddenly it opened, and Da took the opportunity to run out. By dawn, the pursuing cavalry had spread out in all directions; Da lay hidden in the grass.
Since the horsemen did not tread upon the grass, Da remained unharmed within the vegetation and thus escaped the disaster.

Nanta was a man from the Western Regions who was eccentric and unconventional; his conduct was inconsistent, fluctuating between deference and arrogance. Upon entering the borders of Shu, he traveled with three young nuns.

At times he would drink heavily and sing wildly; at other times he would gather crowds to preach the Dharma. The garrison commander of the Shu region detested him deeply and seized Nanta to interrogate him harshly.
Nanta said, "These three nuns are exquisite in song and dance. Thereupon, the garrison commander was pleased and subsequently detained him for the night.

That evening, they set out wine to drink together. They then provided the three nuns with borrowed clothes and garments; furthermore, they bestowed upon them cosmetics and rouge, and they sat in rows to enjoy themselves.

The nuns displayed their graceful charms and playful smiles, putting on their best appearances for the occasion. When the drinking was nearly half-finished and the guests were tipsy, Puṇyavanta said, "May we invite the three nuns to dance?"
The nuns then proceeded to dance, all of them performing with exquisite skill. Dharmatā said, "These women are possessed by demons.
He then seized the sword of a garrison soldier and struck off the heads of the three nuns; the blood flowed for several zhang. The garrison soldier was greatly alarmed, and his attendants bound him.

Dharmatā said, "Do not be so hasty. Look at the three nuns—they are actually *khaṭvāṅga* staffs. The blood is simply the wine they drank earlier. (He bestowed his countenance upon the world, yet others harbored doubts.)

Her appearance was such that she eclipsed all others in the world. The *Youyang zazu* records this incident, stating: "The three nuns sat together; their speech was playful and their graceful demeanor transcended the world.
Fayan was a "Tiger of the Vinaya," while Huirong was a "Dragon of Meaning.
Fayan was a person of the Sui dynasty and is not the same as the Fayan who lived during the earlier Song period. Fayan greatly elucidated the *Vinaya-piṭaka*. To the east...

Xià Shèng transmitted the teachings extensively and understood their meanings with profound clarity; his eloquence was so lofty that even Gāogão and Dūndùn could not rival him, and he was thus titled "The Tiger of the Vinaya.

Huìróng resided at Zhuāngyán Monastery in Yǔxié during the Chen dynasty; his expositions were versatile and expansive, and he attained a deep mastery of the Tripiṭaka, earning him renown throughout the world.

Yiliang, at that time, the Dhyāna Master Zhiyi was preaching the Dharma. Daorong came specifically to pose questions, launching a continuous stream of inquiries through frequent citations and challenges.
Master Zhiyi’s responses arose with sharp precision, illuminating both principle and phenomena. Daorong, who had been self-congratulatory, brandished his fan, but it suddenly fell to the ground.
Master Zhiyi said to Daorong, "The power of meditative concentration cannot be challenged. At that moment, the great assembly mocked Daorong.
He said, "The 'Dragon of Meaning' who has long been renowned is now but a crouching deer. Since the fan has already fallen to the ground, what is there left to hide one's shame?
Yung was deeply ashamed and withdrew. Fajin offered his body, and Sengfu carved his chest.

Fajin made the recitation of the Dharma his primary vocation. During a famine in the Song dynasty when the state granaries were nearly exhausted, Fajin repeatedly begged for food to relieve the hunger of the people.
Later, when there was nowhere left to seek alms, he bathed himself, took a knife and salt, and went to where the starving were gathered.
He bestowed the words of the Dharma upon them one by one, hung his robes on a tree, and threw himself before the hungry, saying: [“Take this!”]
"I give you this food to eat together. Although the crowd was starving and exhausted, they could not bear it out of righteousness.

He stepped forward and cut off his own flesh, seasoned it with salt, and gave it to them to eat until his skin was entirely gone. He said to the hungry ones, "If the King comes, you may offer my bones to him.
Indeed, before long, the Emperor of Song heard of this and came to see; both ruler and subjects wailed and wept. Thereupon, he bestowed three hundred *hu* of wheat upon them.
He rescued those who were starving. (The character "ye" [karma] follows; there is occasionally the character "shi" [time]. If it is "Guo Wang," the character "yu" [day] precedes it.

Sengfu was a native of Gaoyang. In his youth, while still a layman, his family was poor; he constantly applied himself to his studies, gathering firewood to serve as candles for reading by their light.
Later, he went with Xi Zuochi to attend a lecture by Dao’an, and through that occasion, he attained great enlightenment. He became a monk.
Thereafter, he went into hiding in the wilds. At that time, a band of robbers in a village had captured a young boy, intending to extract his heart and liver to offer as a sacrifice to a deity.
On the road, the wealthy man encountered these robbers and inquired in detail about their intentions. He then took off his own clothes to trade for the boy, but the robbers would not agree.
The wealthy man asked, "Can the five internal organs of an adult be used? The robbers replied, "They would be fine. The wealthy man said, "In that case, we must have one..."
He died. His death saved others; though he was dead, he was as if alive. He then took a robber’s knife and sliced from his chest to his navel.
The robbers were greatly alarmed and immediately returned the child to his home. Passersby saw that his wealth remained intact;
they sewed his intestines with needles and applied medicinal ointment, after which he recovered after a long time.
*Shishi Mengqiu* (The Shishi Primer), Volume Lower.
Written by the Śramaṇa Lingcao, who lectures on the teachings at Zhe-shui.
Hui Lin of Xi encountered Yang Hu at Jiao; Ke Yu faced the wall while Hui Lin was in seclusion.
During the Wude era, he lived hidden among the wild grasses. One day, he suddenly met Yang Hu.

After the master and disciple saw one another, they sat together in the fields and conversed as if nothing had changed since their former acquaintance. Each remarked that it had been eight hundred years since they last parted from the Master.
At that time, people everywhere circulated stories about them, yet no one could fathom their divine nature.
Huike and Daoyu lived with Master Bodhidharma on Mount Shaoshi, serving him for seven or eight years.
Bodhidharma then bestowed upon the two masters, Huike and Daoyu, the contemplation of facing a wall. The world has since called this the "Facing the Wall" practice of Shaolin.
He dwelt in seclusion for seven years. As for the eastward spread of the Dhyāna method, Bodhidharma was its beginning (though some accounts, such as the *Chuan*, state four or five years).
[The character] "yi" (change/easy) refers to Fakan. Fakan was skilled in medicine; Tanyuan was marvelous at divination.

Fakan excelled in all the sūtras and vinayas, his understanding of their meaning surpassing that of others, and he was also proficient in medical arts. He frequently begged for alms in the capital, where he encountered...
The wife of a certain family was in critical condition. The attendants treated her without success. Daokai said, "This is easily cured.
The host had already finished slaughtering a sheep, intending to perform a licentious sacrifice. Daokai took a small portion of the sheep's placenta, made it into a broth, and served it to her.

He then applied acupuncture to her vital points. In a short while, the child emerged. Furthermore, during the Shengping era of the Jin dynasty, Emperor Xiaozong fell ill. An edict summoned Daokai to provide medical treatment. Daokai...

While taking the Emperor’s pulse, he refused to administer medicine. Empress Kang issued an order, saying: "The Emperor is slightly unwell, yet Master Kai declines to provide medicinal treatment out of hesitation.
He should be arrested and handed over to the Minister of Justice. Shortly thereafter, the Emperor passed away; thus, [the Empress's judgment] proved remarkably prescient.

Tán Qiān was born into a family of noble and distinguished lineage. At the age of thirteen, he followed his maternal uncle, Quán Huì—who served as the Zhōngsàn Dàfū (Grand Master for the Palace Attendants) under the Qi dynasty—to study the classics and ancient records extensively, while attaining profound mastery of the *Zhòu Yī* (Book of Changes). Huì subsequently transmitted the *Yìxiàng* (Images of the Changes) to Qiān. At that time, there was a woman who had lost an object.

Huì performed a divination for her, but the result yielded no specific image (*xiàng*). He instructed Qiān to interpret it. Qiān replied immediately: "If we judge according to the divination, it is certain..."
A gold hairpin was lost. The old woman was surprised and delighted, saying, "It is truly as you have discerned. Sengqian said, "The character 'dui' (兌) corresponds to the position of metal.

Its two strokes at the bottom extend downward, resembling a gold hairpin. He then instructed her to examine the thief more closely. Sengqian said, "The one who lost it was a white-complexioned girl from the western house with her hair tied in a topknot;
she must be about fifteen or sixteen years old and is the thief. The old woman immediately searched for her and found her; indeed, it was so.
As he had said, Hui asked him the reason for this. Quan replied: "Dui represents the position of the young maiden in the west; among the five colors assigned to the directions, the west is white.
The two dots above the character 'Dui' represent the image of braided hair, and its pointed shape represents the appearance of the mouth being raised.

Hui then held this in high regard. (Note: "Fengkou" likely should be "Bǎngkǒu," pronounced "fèng"; it refers to the high, protruding form of the mouth. Alternatively, is the character "bǎng" being split here to form the word "fengkou"?)
Sengyuan built a bridge; Yinfeng threw his staff at Sengyuan.
Sengyuan’s family was originally very wealthy. When Yüan was first born, the heavens rained coins into his house. The people of Shu marveled at this.
When Yüan grew up, his spirit and demeanor were extraordinary, so [his parents] had him enter the Way. He studied the methods of Chan extensively. Yüan saw [the situation in] Shu...
The waves of the Mian River are unfathomable, and many have perished in its waters. He wished to construct a flying bridge across the southern road;

as soon as these words were spoken, the necessary preparations gathered in abundance. In the past, Zhuge Wuhou had spanned the river with the Seven-Star Bridge, fashioning three iron mallets to strike the bridge pillars, which he subsequently cast into the river once their use was complete.
As they were now constructing the bridge over the deep pool and were about to strike the pillars, the iron mallets—
He floated naturally upon the water as he approached it. When the bridge was completed, he suddenly drowned.

Huìfēng had practiced the path since childhood and resided on Mount Wutai. Later, while traveling by mountain road to join the forces of Huaisi, he encountered the military hostilities of Wú Yuánjì, who was in rebellion against the royal command.
As the government troops and the rebels were engaged in battle with neither side yet having achieved victory or defeat, Huìfēng said:
The crowd said, "I shall go to resolve this slaughter. He then tossed his alms-bowl into the air and flew away with his body.

Arriving above the two opposing ranks, the warriors each beheld the divine monk soaring through the sky; they all withdrew their spears and sheathed their blades, retreating in astonishment and wonder.
(Mò) Níngshī ate lotus roots; Sēnghǎn (the *Fānyìjí* reads Sēngshàn) ate stones.
As for Níngshī, his personal name was lost, and he was called by his clan name. He lived constantly in the mountains and wilds to study the Way. One day, he suddenly died.
After three days he revived. The assembly was astonished and questioned him, and he replied: "I entered the underworld and beheld the various manifestations of the hells.
An official there said to me, 'The Master has a long life but no fortune,' and then ordered a messenger to lead me into the various offices.
An officer there conducted an audit and said, 'The Master has only three *shí* of dried lotus leaves remaining.'"

He recorded this in a register and then released him back to the mountains. From that time on, after his soul had returned, he sustained himself through day and night by eating only dried lotus roots.
The people of Qīn and Lǒng called him the "Monk Who Enters Hell," frequently inviting him to enter the underworld to observe the good and evil deeds of others.
Sengxi resided at Mount Mādura (Mǎtóushān) to practice dhyāna meditation. Later, he suddenly fell gravely ill.
He told his disciples, "I suffer from a cold accumulation within my intestines. In my youth, while living in the mountains to train, my provisions were completely exhausted;
I had nothing left but to eat small pebbles to sustain myself day and night. This resulted in this illness. After I die, you may open my belly to look inside, so as to verify that I indeed ate them."
Shi Er (錫爾). Zhiyan Nengjun (智巖能軍). Huizhi Jian Di (慧璡健敵). Zhiyan’s surname was Hua (華).
From his youth, he possessed military strategy; he was fierce and formidable, difficult to oppose. During the Daye era, among the various states of the illegitimate Zheng (偽鄭)...
The points of the soldiers' weapons rose up in competition. The Grand General, Duke Huang Guo, was leading the expeditionary force.
The Duke said, "Without General Hua, there is no one who can withstand them. At that time, the men and horses of the false state of Zheng were fully equipped.

He held his reins, raised his whip, and thrust his spear into the ground, saying in a stern voice, "If you can pull this out, only then shall we settle our dispute. Yan then mounted his horse, tucked the spear under his armpit, and galloped away.

Tao Biao engaged him in combat until his weapons were exhausted; Sheng then shattered the rocks and captured him. He released him after a short while, whereupon [Tao Biao] was moved to realization and left the household life.
He attained a profound understanding of the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
Huizhi (Huijin) entered the monastic life at the age of seven and specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka. During the Daye era, she resided at Chanding Monastery in a remote wilderness.
One evening, a band of marauders arrived in great numbers to plunder. Huizhi gathered the community and constructed a defensive watchtower to confront them.
At that time, the soldiers unfurled their banners for ten li, and they looted the villages entirely; many were killed. Huizhi then entered the ranks of the enemy. The bandits...
None dared to face his spearhead. The rebels each took Zhen’s hand and said, "A heroic man of the Way! You are truly skilled at battling the enemy.
