(Ma) Shigao transformed a python; Mingchen changed a snake.
An Shiqing, style name Shigao, was the crown prince of the King of Parthia (Anxi). He had extensively collected the classical scriptures and possessed great knowledge and insight.

When his father passed away and he was about to succeed to the throne, Anqing instead vanished from sight and entered the monastic life. He was thoroughly proficient in the sūtras and śāstras; he knew every detail of his past lives.
Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Ling of the Jin dynasty, when chaos broke out due to military unrest in Luoyang, he traveled to Mount Lu and said to the assembly, "I am leaving."
He crossed over to visit his former classmate. They traveled to the temple of Qiongting Lake, which was greatly possessed of spiritual power; merchants and travelers would go there to offer prayers.
The deity then descended and addressed the priest, saying: "There is a śramaṇa on board; you may invite him to come up. Qing then built a shrine for the deity. The deity said:
"In the past, I left the household life and studied the Way alongside you, Master. I practiced much in giving, yet I was prone to great anger.
I am now the deity of Gongting Temple; a thousand li all around are under my jurisdiction. My current body is that of a python; after my death, I shall enter hell."
Faqing asked, "Why do you not manifest your form? The python suddenly appeared, weeping like falling rain.
It said to Faqing, "I pray that you, Master, will deliver me. I have a thousand bolts of silk and various treasures; please use them to build a temple so that I may be reborn in a good realm.
Faqing then took the goods and led him away. As the python climbed the mountain to look back, he wished to return to Yuzhang to build the temple. By evening, there was one...
A youth boarded the boat and knelt before Qing, saying: "The spirit of Mount Qiuting has already left its evil form; thus, its temple no longer possesses divine efficacy.
People saw a dead python on the western mountainside, over ten li in length; this is the present-day She Village (Śe-cūn) of Xunyang.
(The "Ling" of Jin should be "Ling" of Han.)
Wei Mingchen was a man of great learning whose eloquence was vast and profound. Initially, he composed the "Snake Formation Method" (*she shì fǎ*), which circulated widely in the eastern provinces;
this method was like Zhuge Liang’s military formations. At that time, a person from Shangyi in Luzhou wished to propagate the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He traveled to Linlü County in Yanzhou to invite a monk who could lecture on it, and upon returning, he preached the *Lotus Sūtra*. When Wei Mingchen, an old acquaintance of his, heard of this, he went there as well.
He challenged him with difficult questions. Seeing that Tanbin’s eloquence and reasoning were so versatile and formidable, the monk felt inwardly anxious and conflicted.

He then approached Tanbin with sincere courtesy and said, "This district has recently begun to place its faith in the Buddhist scriptures, and the local scholars have turned their hearts toward them. I pray that the Great Dharma Master will join us in supporting and promoting them."
"I venture to offer ten rolls of silk to the Dharma Master. Sengchen accepted them. The next day, when he wished to attend a lecture from the high seat, the monk became even more terrified.

When it was time for the lecture, Sengchen tied up his silk, entered the hall, and said to the assembly, "Yesterday, the High Seat Dharma Master presented me with silk and requested that I not discuss the principles of the Dharma.
However, the Buddha-dharma is vast and profound, and one must distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Thereupon, he proceeded to debate with him.

As for the meaning [of the text], Sengchen’s eloquence and exposition were not equal to that of the monk; moreover, his understanding of the doctrine was不通 (not thorough). The assembly all laughed loudly.
Sengchen immediately left the town, while his two companions felt such indignation and frustration that their breath was choked. For several days they were ashamed and silent.

Eventually, they climbed a mountain and sat beneath a tree, where one said to his companion, "I am now so feverish with distress that I fear I might transform into a snake. He then untied his clothes, bared his body, and stretched out his two legs. Suddenly—
It transformed into the shape of a snake. One companion climbed a tree to escape it, and then said to his other two companions, "I regret having debated about snakes;
it has truly come to this. His companions were greatly terrified and fled to Ye (Yecheng) to tell the story. (One companion—this should likely be read as "two companions.")
Fahzhi, whose secular surname was Bai, and Daosun, whose secular surname was Linghua, both followed the Dharma.
Fahzhi entered the gates of the Empty Gate (Buddhism) at a young age and cultivated the principles of meditation with clarity. Later, on the day of his death, he instructed the assembly:
"You may expose my remains beneath the pines to feed the birds and beasts. After his passing, several divine banners were suddenly seen in the sky, descending from the west.
He came to welcome [the deceased]. The bamboo groves surrounding the monastery were lush and verdant, yet at that moment, their colors all turned white.
Daosun had mastered the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras since his tonsure; later, he dwelt in the mountains and wilds to study Buddhist scriptures, eventually passing away there in his old age.
After his death, his body remained on the mountain peak for a night, during which time spiritual flowers suddenly appeared, encircling him on all sides.
A stem two feet long sprang up from the earth, its color and form fresh and radiant. At that time, there was a hunter who did not believe;

he sought to see this flower, but by the time he arrived, it had already vanished. He wept and said, "In life I did not receive the opening of faith, and in death I do not receive the auspicious omen of this flower.

How utterly unresponsive you are! If there is a sign in the way of the divine, I pray that you manifest your numinous form once more. As soon as he finished speaking, the spiritual flower burst forth again from the earth.
The hunter then sent word that he was leaving the household life.
Tongjin drank wine; Wuzhuo sipped tea.
Tongjin left home at a young age and did not observe the monastic rules, loving only to drink wine. He said to others, "Wine can be used for libation."
He was of average stature. When he became intoxicated, he would urinate, leaving behind foul odors and filth; everyone despised him.
It happened that when Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou campaigned in the east, he was fond of poisonous drugs. He issued an edict for Luzhou to manufacture poisoned wine.

The supervising officials diligently gathered dozens of varieties, including the head of a viper, the root of the *tiexing*, large bees, wild yam (*dage*), and the feathers of a *zheng* bird. These were brewed in an iron vat. Once the medicine was prepared, [he] donned leather...

One must wear lapis lazuli robes to shield the eyes before one may approach it; otherwise, its vapors will strike the person and cause death. When the medicine touches a human, the flesh is pierced and destroyed.
Jin heard of this and went to the supervising official to request a drink. The official said, "If you can drink a single cup, are you not a man of wine?"

Sengjin said, "I can drink as much as you wish. He then took an iron ladle and repeatedly scooped from the medicinal jar to drink. Monastics and laypeople were struck with wonder and came to watch him.
Sengjin continued to take more than ten ladles of liquid and drank it all without his facial expression changing at all.

He sighed to himself, saying, "Only now have I finally managed to get one drunkenness. People fled to avoid him. A short while later, he lay down upon a square stone and suddenly urinated on the garment he was wearing.
The rocks all split and shattered. When he advanced and woke up, everything was as it had been before;
there was no trace of the damage. Beyond his regular practice of listening to and studying the teachings, he once traveled to Mount Wutai wishing to observe its sacred traces.
He then performed prostrations while gazing toward the Vajra Cave, whereupon he sat down upon a rock and fell asleep. Suddenly, he heard the sound of a cowherd shouting "Drink water! three times.
Then he saw an old man of ancient appearance, coarse and ugly in form, wearing a short coarse cloth tunic and trailing sandals.

The man took him by the hand and said, "I have come here from outside the mountains seeking provisions. Are you weary from sleeping here, Master? Zhe replied, "No. The man said, "If you are not weary..."

"Why are you sleeping so abruptly? Zhe said, "Ordinary people are mired in dullness; how can this be considered strange? The old man said, "If you, Master, are so dull, would it not be better for you to go and drink some tea?
He then pointed toward the monastery. Zhe followed him, stepping along with difficulty, until they reached the temple gate.
The old man called out "Kuntī" three times. A boy responded, appearing to be fourteen or fifteen years old, with hair hanging down to his shoulders and wearing—

He was dressed in coarse cloth. The grounds of his temple were all made of lapis lazuli, and the halls and buildings were golden. The old man sat upon a white-toothed couch and provided a brocade cushion for [the monk] to sit upon.

After a short while, a youth brought two bowls of tea; they drank from them together until finished. Then, the old man lifted a tortoise-shell vessel filled with cream and curd, giving a spoonful to each.
They drank it and swallowed it, as if there were something to be realized, whereupon they attained clear awakening with sudden clarity.
(Hui Bu expounded the principles of the Dharma; Fa Tai refuted heterodoxy. Hui Bu, in his youth, entered the monastic order under Dharma Master Qiong to study the Way.
His understanding and practice were lofty and brilliant, and he was eloquent in exposition.
He was difficult to defeat. Later, he debated the teachings with Meditation Master Miao for three days; as their discussion in the assembly continued without end, Miao eventually yielded to him.
Huibù also came down [from his seat] at that time. During the rebellion of Hou Jing, there was famine for several years.
Huibù did not eat for three days; on the fourth day, someone gave him a small amount of rice covered with a thin layer of meat broth, yet although his stomach—
He maintained his resolve and refused to eat, like a fire burning.
Fata was a contemporary student of Dao’an during his youth; he possessed great insight and awakening. He stood eight chi tall, with a dignified and elegant bearing.

At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Daochang who possessed considerable talent and ability. He constantly adhered to the doctrine of "no meaning" (wuyi) and widely propagated it throughout the land of Jing.
Fatai said, "This is a heterodox teaching and must be refuted. He then convened a great assembly of renowned monks and ordered Tanyi to challenge him with difficult questions.
Daochang relied on scriptural citations and logical arguments to debate with him from every perspective; Huiyuan was constantly bested. The next day, they gathered again for Huiyuan to take his seat.
After several rounds of refutation, Guan’s sharp points began to emerge. Daochang then felt that the course of the argument had shifted into a different realm;

he struck the table with his fly-whisk, yet no answer emerged. Huiyuan said, "Without haste, yet swift—why do you keep shifting and rearranging? Those present laughed heartily. Daochang was disheartened.

The meaning of "non-existence" ceases from this point onward. (Regarding "difficulties," it should be "attacks and difficulties. Regarding "Guan Gui," it is likely a corruption of "questioning and reprimanding. Regarding "the Way is constant," the commentary reads "the Way is eternal. Regarding "shu and zhou," the commentary reads "zhu and yu"; their pronunciations are interchangeable.

"Zhu" is pronounced like *chù*, referring to the shuttle that moves the warp on a loom; colloquially called a *suō*. It is related to the character "zhou. As for the character "yu," it belongs to the class of tangerines (*jú*), but they share the same pronunciation.
One should take the modern text as correct. (Yu) De-su was naturally unremarkable; Hui-leng attained awakening in his youth.

Huìyuē (慧約), courtesy name Dêsù (德素), was surnamed Lóu (樓) and a native of Dōngyáng (東陽). His mother, Lady Liú (劉氏), became pregnant after dreaming that a man held up a golden image for her to swallow and seeing purple light encircling her body;
thus she gave birth to him. By the age of seven, Huìyuē was already proficient in the classics and histories, whereupon he sought to leave the secular life.
By nature, he favored the profound mysteries of the doctrine and traveled extensively to visit renowned masters to study the scriptural teachings. He attained great mastery.
Mingwu. A popular song from the eastern region says: "The youth who attained the subtle principle was Layman Lou Hui-leng.
Hui-leng’s surname was Shen; his secular family name was Tu. He was a native of Xiyin. His father died while he was still in the womb, and his mother raised him alone.
When he reached the age of three, he said to his mother, "I wish to hear the Dharma. Out of pity for her son's orphaned suffering, his mother took him along to listen to the teachings in Xiangyang.

Dharma Master Yang Run lectured on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises). After listening, [Huiyuan] attained a profound understanding of the meanings within the texts, which caused the assembly to marvel and exclaim in praise.
He sought only to leave the household life, but his mother, being solitary and alone, did not permit it. When he reached the age of eight, his mother passed away;
he then went to Vinaya Master Dan to seek ordination and became profoundly enlightened in the Tripitaka.
Senghui Crosses the River; Anjing Ascends the Tomb. Senghui was in Jingzhou.
Liu Qiu of Nanyang established Zhiqui Temple and invited Senghui to reside there. Senghui frequently went to the riverbank, where a ferry official requested a toll for crossing.
The ferry official pressed him, saying the boat was too small to carry him across. In an instant, he flew through the air.
As he passed, [the ferryman] saw him on both banks; the ferry official was greatly astonished and knew him to be a sage. (In one version of the text, the character for "ferry" is absent.)
Sengjing was traveling eastward. Upon reaching Dingtao, he asked directly, "Where is Layman Ding? The local villagers all replied, "He has been dead for three years;
his burial is in the outskirts. Sengjing said, "This man was a bodhisattva living at home. He then went to the site of the grave and dug it up himself.
At that moment, five-colored clouds rose from atop the tomb, a magnificent omen worthy of being beheld. And so it was...
He took the bones; they were all golden in color, linked together like a chain about five *zhang* long. When shaken, they produced a resonant sound (*xiāng*, which should be read as *xiǎng*).
Only when silent did he carry them, hanging them from the tip of his staff, and departed from the local people.
Thus, the upright man produced lotuses. Qiyu treated the tree (the "tree" is pronounced *shù*, with the second tone).
Suizhen was a man of simple and upright character. He made it his constant practice to recite the Lotus Sūtra, never ceasing for even a moment until he reached old age.
Later, he suddenly passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. In an instant, seven stalks of blue lotuses emerged from his mouth.
Jīvaka was a man from India who arrived in Luoyang and widely propagated the teachings of the Dharma. He was friends with Teng Yongwen, the Grand Administrator of Nanyang and Governor of Hengyang.
While residing at Manshui Monastery in Luoyang, he found that several dozen *cintāmaṇi* trees in the monastery had withered and died.
Jīvaka asked Yongwen, "How long has it been since these trees died? Yongwen replied, "It has been many years. Jīvaka—
He immediately recited incantations over it; soon thereafter, it flourished and grew with extraordinary vigor and luxuriance. From this time on, all people marveled at it in admiration.
Pure Deliverance Roams the Hunt; the Mysterious Wind Spreads the Net.

Shi Jundu was rarely occupied with hunting. One day, he shot a pregnant deer and caused it to miscarry; as the mother deer, writhing in pain, licked her offspring on the ground, Jundu attained spiritual awakening through this event.
He immediately broke his bow and snapped his arrows, left the household life to study the Way, and devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna meditation.
He was well-versed in the various classics and had a profound mastery of their deep meanings. (The character "hu" [suddenly] appears below "one day.
Fu Xi, whose courtesy name was Xuānfēng, possessed a steadfast and resolute character from the age of seven.

One day he said to his parents, "I have frequently dreamed of ascending into the void and traveling there, where I often engaged in battle with immeasurable numbers of servants and followers; I always emerged victorious. Later, with...
The local people at Jieting made their living by setting nets and traps; they would sink their cages into the water and recite a prayer:
"Those who wish to leave may go; those who wish to stay may remain. At the time, the people considered them foolish. Later, they encountered the Indian monk Dharmasena, who said to them:
"I once accompanied you to the assembly of Vipaśyin Buddha and we vowed together to deliver sentient beings. Now, your robes and alms bowl still remain in the Tuṣita Heaven. On what day..."
He replied, "I shall return. You may try approaching the water to observe its form. When he did so, he indeed saw a circular halo and jeweled canopies filling his entire body;

thus, he discerned the cause of his previous life. He then asked Sōng about the methods for cultivating the Way. Sōng pointed to the summit of Mount Sōng and said, "This is where you may take up residence.
Later, Hsi left behind extraordinary traces.
Sengcan of the Three Kingdoms Period. Dao, the nineteenth patriarch of the Nine Provinces, was Sengcan.
From his youth, he revered the Way and prioritized traveling to study. There were no sacred sites throughout the world that he did not visit and seek out.

He frequently entered the three kingdoms of Qi, Chen, and Wei; wherever there was a center for the Dharma, he never failed to visit. He would sometimes expound upon the scriptural teachings of the Tripiṭaka.

He instructed [his disciples] and engaged them in debate and citation. Furthermore, he was profoundly versed in the Confucian tradition and established his fame throughout the four seas, styling himself the "Master of Discourse on the Three Kingdoms.
Daoyi, from his youth, transcended the mundane world; he was upright and exceptional, possessing a majestic and far-reaching spirit. He followed Fatai to study the profound [teachings].

Having thoroughly investigated both internal and external teachings, he later traveled east to Shanyin to lecture on various sūtras and śāstras. At that time, monks and nuns from all nine provinces came to study under him.
His contemporaries called him "Little Yi," and the Master served as the *karmadāna* (administrative director) for the nine provinces.
Zhentiao was a toad, and Tante was a monkey.
Zhentiao’s home was on Gold Mountain (*Suvarṇaparvata*). For generations his family had been hunters.
One day, while resting in a field after pursuing game, he broke off a willow branch, skewered several toads on it, and placed them in the water to prepare as food. He then returned to the mountains.
While hunting, he had pierced a frog with his arrow and forgotten about it. When he went out on a hunt again the following spring, he heard the croaking of frogs.
Suddenly, he saw that the thirty-odd frogs he had pierced the previous year were still alive. He reported this and, filled with lamentation and self-reproach, exclaimed, "How bitter!
Why did I, for the sake of my own belly, cause them to suffer for so many years? Thereupon, he untied the string, released them, and made a vow to leave the world.

He entered the mountains with his family to practice the Way. Prostrating himself upon the ground, he repented for his former transgressions and subsequently shaved his head and donned the robes to become a monk.
He was moved by Maitreya Bodhisattva, who personally conferred the precepts and the Dharma upon him; Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva personally exhorted and inspired him;
and Maitreya himself bestowed the three robes and other requisites.
During the Later Wei dynasty, there was a man named Tante. Although he had left the household life as a monk, he drank wine and ate meat just like a layman;

his behavior was excessively wild and unrestrained. Whenever he spoke of past events, his words always accorded with human experience. When Emperor Wen of the Northern Zhou heard of him, he sent down an imperial decree specifically to inquire about his affairs.
At that time, Shenwu of the Qi state came to raid Yubie. Tante said, "Will a dog ever reach Longmen? Indeed, it did not reach Longmen.
He returned through the gate. Furthermore, before Hou Jing rebelled, Tuhu suddenly took up a staff with a monkey carved on its head and had him face west, playing with it day and night.
He also asked for a one-horned bow and pulled at it. Shortly thereafter, Hou Jing rebelled, but soon returned to the Liang dynasty.
At that time, people said that the carving of the monkey was an omen of Hou Jing.
Zhirun and Bozhan: Tanyi’s Refinement.
Zhirun resided in Xiangyang where he gave public lectures; he possessed great renown and was profoundly learned both in Buddhist and secular matters.
His eloquence was grand and transcendent, such that his contemporaries all called him "Master Run," and none could surpass Bozhan.

Tanyi possessed a spirit that was clear and refined, and his physical appearance was extraordinary. He was foremost among all those versed in the various vehicles of the teachings in his understanding of their meaning.

He was held in high esteem by Yao Xing, the ruler of the Qin. Seeing how Tanyi surpassed all other scholars, Yao Xing would often say to Kumārajīva, "Master Tanyi is truly a monk who stands as the preeminent model of elegance for this land."
Senglang knew of the theft; Fataong was imprisoned.
During the Jin dynasty, the monk Senglang traveled abroad to study the Way. He was thoroughly versed in the Buddha-vehicle and also took the Confucian classics as his primary school.
Later, while traveling with companions, he suddenly said to them midway through their journey: "Among you, there must be someone who has stolen the robes and bowls from the monastery."
As he was about to depart, his companions did not believe him and returned together to the monastery to search for him; indeed, it was just as he had said.
Fǎtōng was a native of Shílóu in Lóngquán. During his days as a layman, he alone harbored extraordinary aspirations and believed solely in the teachings of Śākyamuni.
One day, he suddenly shaved the heads of his two sons, two daughters, and his wife, encouraging them all to enter the Way, and then departed for the mountains.
He took up residence in a temple and subsequently shaved his head to become a monk. When people asked him the reason for this, he replied, "I have cast off my shackles and chains;
my resolve is to cause the Great Dharma to flourish. Later, he traveled to his home village. The village headman questioned him, to which he replied, "I am a mountain dweller.
Enraged, the headman imprisoned him and forbade him from traveling abroad. Thereupon, he ceased eating and walked in circumambulation around the prison.
When night fell, the sound of wild foxes howling filled the village, and everyone became uneasy. The village headman, finding this strange, said, "There must be a strange monk in the prison.
He then released him. The monk said, "I was practicing the Way and had just attained the flavor of Buddhahood;

why have you released me? In an instant, the foxes' cries ceased, and the villagers were at peace. (The character following "shājiā" [釋枷] has been eaten away by insects; it is unknown what character it was. Judging by the flow of the text, perhaps a character has been omitted.)
(Dao)sheng led his disciples, while Huiyuan formed a religious society.
When Zhu Dao-sheng first entered Mount Lu, he lived in seclusion for ten years to pursue his aspirations. He delved into the sutras and treatises, profoundly investigating their principles;
consequently, his fame filled the world. Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty’s Taizu treated him with profound courtesy and respect. Later, he [Dao-sheng] led...
Accompanied by over a thousand followers, he came to Mount Huqiu in Wu to lecture on and transmit the scriptural teachings.
Some say that during one of Sengsheng’s lectures, there was a strange rock on the mountain that would nod its head as it listened to his discourse.
Although the world refers to this as "Master Sengsheng’s Nodding Rock at Huqiu," the original record has not yet been seen.

Huiyuan studied the Confucian classics from his youth; his spirit was brilliant and refined. At the age of thirteen, he traveled to various regions to pursue his studies, exhausting the Three Piṭakas internally and mastering the Nine Classics externally, while also being well-versed in the works of Zhuangzi and Laozi. He and his younger brother Huidi both took Master Dao’an as their teacher.
Later, he settled at Mount Lu, where famous scholars from all quarters flocked to the mountain gate. Among them were Liu Yimin of Yuzhang and Lei Cizong.
There were one hundred and twenty-three people in total, including Zhou Xuzhi, Bi Yingzhi, Zong Bing, Zhang Laimin, and Zhang Jishuo from Yanmen.

They all renounced worldly glory to pursue the tranquility of the silent realm, taking refuge under Master Huiyuan. They devoted themselves to the study of both Buddhist exoteric and esoteric teachings;
furthermore, they planted white lotuses before the Amitābha Hall at Longquan Temple and established a Pure Land Society. Liu Yimin and others all composed commemorative inscriptions for them.
His life story has been recorded. From the Jin dynasty until the present day, the entire world has transmitted the legend of Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society.
As for Master Xianglu, Master Yong pointed him out as a "horse," and Master Hui recognized him as the leader.
At the age of six, he received full ordination; he attained a profound realization of the scriptural teachings and specialized in upholding the Vinaya. He resided at Xianglin Temple in Shizhou.

At the beginning of the Wude era, Duke Lingyang came to preside over Yizhou. The Duke was of few worldly attachments; with a devoted heart, he traveled with more than a hundred loads of goods until he reached Xianglin Temple.
There, he ordered the donkeys and their loads to be placed within the temple’s Buddha Hall, Sangha Hall, and Lecture Hall.
None dared to disobey. When the host saw this filth and disorder, he entered his room in lamentation and took up his iron staff and the three robes, vowing:
"Whether I live or die today, I rely solely on the power of the protective deities of the precepts to rid myself of these.
He then raised his staff toward the donkeys, and the donkeys suddenly collapsed all at once as if dead. The host then took up one load with each hand and threw them away.
In mid-air, the Duke witnessed this marvel; he then repented and returned to the faith. Huiyong retired to Mount Lu and personally relied upon Huìyuǎn.
He profoundly mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka and was also well-versed in non-Buddhist texts. One day, having left the town at dawn, he returned to the mountain by evening.
Upon reaching Wúqiáo, he encountered a military commander who, intoxicated and riding a vicious horse, blocked the road before him.
Huiyong did not permit the horse to pass. As the sun was about to set, Huiyong pointed at the horse with his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), and the horse bolted.
The camp commander threw it to the ground; Huiyong picked it up, comforted him, and returned him to the camp. On the following day, the commander came to the monastery to repent.
Huiyong said, "It was not my original intention that caused this. I fear it was the work of the deity of the precepts."
Sengda’s Sweet Cakes (Note: "Da" [達] has "duo-mie" [蠹滅] below it; perhaps it is the character "que" [却]?).
Sengda received fruit from Shi Yu and traveled to study in various regions. He practiced meditation and transmitted the Dharma. His teeth were over an inch long, a wondrous feature unlike any other.
Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty held him in high esteem. Later, he resided on Mount Huahuang at Linli, where a mountain deity frequently came to listen to the Dharma. Suddenly...
One night, someone pushed open the door and entered, saying, "I am the wife of the mountain deity. During the day, I have no leisure to pay my respects to the Zen Master;
therefore, I have come today specifically to visit and offer this basket of rice cakes. I pray that when you perform your prostrations before the Buddha, you will call out my name.
Dadao replied, "The rice cakes may be taken back; moreover, I, a mountain monk, do not eat them. However, I shall perform a single prostration for you as I worship the Buddha."
He chanted both [the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna]. The wife of the mountain deity then prostrated and took her leave.
Shi Yu was eight chi and five cun tall, with an extraordinary appearance. Residing at Mount Xiangying in Yizhou, he studied the sūtras and śāstras.
One night, he suddenly dreamed that four dragons flew into his eyes; upon waking, he attained a great realization of the Buddha’s intent.
He constantly dwelt in the mountains, practicing austerities while abstaining from grain. Only four monkeys would gather mountain fruits twice daily to offer him;
Yu accepted them for a long time. (He was eight chi and five cun; tradition records him as eight chi and three cun.
Fa Kuang dispelled the demons, and Hui An prevented calamity.
Zhu Fakang was esteemed and held in high regard by Xie An for his mastery of both Buddhist and secular learning. Fakang frequently resided in mountain forests;

whenever Xie An went there to pay his respects, he found the dwelling place so humble and remote that even carriages and horses could not reach it. Xie An would therefore ascend the mountain peaks on foot. During this time, Sima Daozi, the Prince of Jin, served as Chancellor.

Hearing that Daoxuan was traveling through the wilderness, the Governor of Tangyi and others were dispatched to invite him to the capital to receive offerings. At that time, ominous stars appeared repeatedly;

the Jin Emperor requested Daoxuan to perform a ritual of repentance (*zhāi-chàn*) to avert them. Daoxuan said, "Your Majesty should cultivate profound virtue, and this humble monk shall exhaust his sincerity.
He then entered the ritual of repentance for more than a day. The officials reported that the ominous stars had already vanished.
Huian was traveling in the capital when he saw that the Chancellor Xiu Jing had achieved great merit on the frontier and possessed incomparable wealth and prestige.
Huian went to visit him and said to Jing, "Chancellor, you are indeed magnificent; yet alas, within a few months you shall face a great calamity.
Nevertheless, you may prepare for it in advance. Jing, recognizing Huian’s spiritual attainment and knowing the omen, prostrated himself and informed him [of his situation].
Tao’an went to perform an exorcism for him. An said, “You should seek two large dogs, several feet tall and of fierce disposition.
Once the dogs were obtained, An returned and said, “The matter depends on this very night. That evening, he sat with Jing;
An ordered ten men to stand by the side of the seat, holding bows and arrows. When the night grew deep, An said with a smile, “Your Excellency’s calamity has been averted.”
At dawn, he called Jing and went together into the garden. There they saw a thief holding a sword who had already been killed, with blood flowing from his neck.
They also saw two dogs beneath a large tree barking upward at another thief, who likewise held a great sword.
Seeing Jing, the thief cried out, "I and those others are all resentful toward the Chancellor; we came intending to harm him. He is crouching in ambush, so we cannot advance."
Daojing was greatly alarmed and said to Dao’an, “Had it not been for my Master’s prior knowledge, I would have perished at the hands of those two men.
(Yang) Daogang and Yihù; Gongming Zhináng and Daogang.
While in Jiangdong, Daogang exhaustively researched the sūtras and śāstras; his mastery of their principles was so comprehensive that everyone of the time held him in high esteem. Thus, the East—

Nanmu was styled Yihù. Zhīqián, courtesy name Gōngmíng, was a person from Yuezhi. He came to travel in the land of Hán and extensively propagated the teachings of the Dharma. He was profoundly learned in the scriptures and treatises.
As a man, he was slender and tall with a dark complexion; his eyes were mostly white with yellow pupils. People of the time said of him, "The eyes of Master Zhī."
Zhong Huang: Although his physical frame was small, he was a treasury of wisdom. He was a man of the Han period.
His spiritual essence was as level as the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*), and his profound brilliance shone from his eyes.

At the age of seven, Zhong Huang had already memorized and mastered the classics and histories, and he was also proficient in literary composition. He passed the examination for "Child Geniuses" (*tóngzi jǔ*) with honors. Upon reaching...
He was advanced in years and held a high official rank. Renouncing his glory to enter the Way, he devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna and propagated its teachings during his time.
Later, while traveling through Wei-yang and reaching the road at Liu-he, he suddenly sighed that the Great Dharma was in decline and that he had not lived to meet a Buddha.
After a short while, he heard a voice from the air saying: "Open the ground of your mind, and you shall see the Bodhisattva in the form of the wondrous Mañjuśrī. He then...

Tàn raised his neck and pressed it with his palm; immediately, red marks appeared on his four fingers. This seal remained constantly visible, and Tàn said, "This must be the heart-seal (citta-mudrā) bestowed upon me by a Great Sage."
Xuanchang was still a layman in his youth when his entire family was annihilated by the Hu barbarians.

As they were about to kill him, the barbarian leader saw him and stopped them, saying, "This boy’s gaze is piercing; he is no ordinary child. He was thus spared. Later, he left the household life and became a monk.
Guangtong was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular learning. While traveling to Liangzhou, he encountered a cruel barbarian regime that suppressed the Buddha-dharma and slaughtered the monastics.
Only Guangtong managed to escape; fleeing from the mountains and valleys of Daijun, he crossed the Great Wall and turned south toward Mengjin.

Carrying nothing but a bundle of willow twigs and a handful of scallion leaves, he was nearly overtaken by the barbarian cavalry. Placing the scallion leaves into his nostrils, he entered the river and swam across.
Meng Jin was released from his post. Emperor Wen of Song, knowing that Sengchang’s Way was practiced, summoned him;

he was appointed as Grand Master to the Crown Prince, but he declined and did not accept. [Note: "Lü shuài" (ruler of the barbarians)—the first character is pronounced "shuāi," meaning general. If pronounced "lǜ," it refers to the troops one commands.
○ Dàjùn should be Dàijùn. Daojie had a large head; Wenxing had long eyebrows.

Daojie’s surname was Yang; he was a descendant of Yang Zhen, the Grand Marshal of the Han dynasty. His physical appearance was imposing and refined, and he possessed a highly adept manner of response.

Furthermore, he was thoroughly versed in the sutras and treatises, possessing broad learning in both scholarship and literary composition. He was fair-skinned with a large head, so those in Bingzhou called him "Da-tou-jie" (Big-Headed Jie).
He was difficult to defeat in debate; indeed, his profound meaning—each inquiry and each reproof—could cause others to break into a sweat.

Sengxing was a monk from the state of Qi who traveled to spread the Dharma at Mount Ju in Muzhou. After his death, people marveled at the place where he lived and called it Xing Gongdui (The Mound of Master Xing).
Xing’s eyebrows were over a foot long and hung down over his face; whenever he wished to see an object, he would [lift them up].
Vijaya was skilled in heterodox arts. Tanyuan [Tánluán] possessed the elixirs of the immortals;
he surpassed Vijaya. Vijaya had long venerated heterodox arts, making the worship of fire his profession. At that time, a śramaṇa arrived and requested a night's lodging. Vijaya—

He was not permitted [to enter]. The śramaṇa then sat out in the open air by the gate and stayed the night. He secretly applied divine incantations (*dhāraṇī*), and the fire he served suddenly vanished.
The entire family welcomed him back and repented their errors; they then believed in the spiritual efficacy of the Śākya teachings.
Thereupon, they joined the śramaṇa to leave the household life. Entering the borders of Han, he translated the sūtras and vinaya extensively.
Tanduan resided at Mount Wutai. Having been afflicted by a heart ailment, he said: "Life is precarious and fragile; its constancy cannot be taken for granted.
Would it not be well to seek the methods of the immortals to prolong one's life? Once that goal is achieved, one may then revere the Buddha-dharma."
He then traveled south to the residence of Tao Yinyu to seek his immortal formulas.

Indeed, he met Yinyu, who bestowed upon him ten scrolls of immortal formulas, intended as arts for extending one's lifespan. As Sengluan was about to arrive at Luoyang, he encountered the Chinese Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci.
Sengluan went to him and said, "Within the Buddha-dharma, there exists this method for longevity and immortality; it is superior to this [Daoist method]."
Regarding the "recipe of the Earthly Immortal," Sengliu spat on the ground and said, "What kind of talk is this? It is not comparable [to the truth].
Where in this world is there a gate to longevity and immortality? Even if one were to extend the span of years, the cycle of saṃsāra would never cease.

He then bestowed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* upon Sengluan, saying, "This is the recipe of the Great Immortal. If you practice according to it, you shall surely attain liberation from birth and death."—Sengluan.

He then burned ten scrolls of alchemical formulas and thereby attained great enlightenment in the Buddha-vehicle. At that time, among the monks who expounded the meanings of the scriptures in the capital of Wei, Tanluan was the foremost.
The Wei ruler held him in high esteem and bestowed upon him the title Shenluan (the tradition states his name was also written as Tanluan; furthermore, the character for "luan" is not fixed).
Master Cen Raised Mice; Master Dao-pan Released Sheep.
As for Dharma Master Cen, he was exceptionally observant of the precepts and could recite over five hundred scrolls of the sutras; this is how laypeople addressed him.
He resided on Mount Sangai, where it was his constant practice to wear silk robes and beg for food. Any food remaining over was used to feed the mice in his quarters.
Hundreds of mice came to him; Xian was so thoroughly tamed by them that they would nestle closely against his peak.
If any mouse fought with or bit another, Xian would immediately reprimand it until it changed its behavior. If any mouse fell ill, Xian would rub it with his hand, and it would be healed.
Daojian was profoundly learned in both Confucianism and Buddhism and was highly esteemed in his time.

In the first year of the Qianming era of the Qi dynasty, he set out from the capital of Ye with more than twenty companions, intending to travel to the Western Regions. Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou granted him an official letter and provided funds for his journey.
Upon reaching the country of the Turks, he again requested an official letter. When he arrived at the country of Xikehan, they did not recognize him as a śramaṇa and intended to...
They inflicted further harm and increased the number of guards, yet provided no grain. They merely intended for them to die of starvation.
At that time, there was a Chinese envoy there who admonished Ke Han, saying, "These are disciples of the Buddha. In their home country, the Son of Heaven greatly promotes their teaching.
Ke Han then came to believe in and respect them, providing four sheep daily to supply the regular food for Pan and the others. Pan then led them out from the ground.
He was released. Although he reached the height of starvation, he ate nothing but wild grasses and vegetables gathered daily by himself.
Regarding Baoqiong Longrui and Hui zhe Xiangwang:

since Baoqiong received full ordination, his extraordinary deeds were most manifest; his lectures were versatile and his mastery of the principles of the teachings profound. Emperor Gao of the Liang dynasty...

The Patriarch invited him to the capital to perform rites and offerings. Later, while he was instructing his disciples at Jian’an Temple, one day young and old began clamoring together, vying to say that a white dragon had appeared at the Jian’an Vihāra. They all rushed to the temple, but saw only Dharma Master Juǎng seated there, delivering a lecture.
Officials, nobles, and commoners alike exclaimed, "At Jian’an, the auspicious sign of the dragon has soared forth; this is the Way of Dharma Master Juǎng."
Was this not the result of his past conduct? Consequently, he was titled Master Baiqiong (White Jade). His wisdom was profound and his learning vast;

he mastered the various sūtras and investigated their subtle meanings with great precision. His fame resounded throughout the world, and all looked up to him in reverence. Furthermore, his gait was measured and orderly, and his gaze was steady without wandering;
his deportment resembled that of an elephant king. Thus, the people of the world collectively referred to him as the "Elephant King."
Zhe (Wu).
Mingzhan stood upright with his body straight; Tanyuan raised his feet in reverence.

Mingzhan possessed extraordinary character from his youth and was proficient in both internal and external learning. At the beginning of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, the Emperor had returned from the Southern Suburban Sacrifice.

In the capital, there was at that time a corrupt monk. The Emperor grew angry and summoned him, ordering that he be made to prostrate before the representatives of the two traditions of Śākyamuni and Laozi. Daohan heard of this and went to remonstrate with the Emperor.

The Emperor was greatly incensed, and the representative of the Laozi tradition immediately took his leave. The Emperor intended to impose legal punishment upon Daohan, but Daohan stood firm and confronted him directly.
Realizing that the teaching of Gautama was profound and solemn, and perceiving that Daohan’s resolve was lofty and upright, the Emperor promptly rescinded the edict.
Tanyǎn initially traveled to Yecheng, where he had no fixed place of residence. Whenever there was a Dharma assembly, he would invariably ascend the lecture seat to expound the sutras.

During the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty, followers of Buddhism and Daoism vied with one another over their relative superiority. The Daoist Lu Xiujing arbitrarily engaged in sophistry and fabrication;
consequently, the Emperor issued an edict for the śramaṇas and Daoists to compete in their respective magical arts. At that time, the Daoists cast spells upon the śramaṇas.
His robes and alms bowl flew about, crossing and turning; the Daoist thus displayed such supernatural powers himself. He said, "The Śramaṇa manifests one, I shall manifest two.
The Emperor ordered the Master Shangtong to compete with Xiu Jing. Shangtong said, "Artificial techniques are not worth testing.
He also ordered a monk from the very bottom rank to debate with the Senior Preceptor (Upādhyāya). Xian took the bottom seat. [He was] intoxicated.
He was so intoxicated that he had to be supported as he moved toward his seat; the assembly all laughed at him.

Xian said to Li Zong, "Regarding what you previously boasted about my ability to manifest supernatural feats—one or two—there is indeed deep meaning in this. He then stood upon the seat, balancing on one leg.
"I have already manifested one; you should manifest two. Each remained speechless in response. Xian said, "Just now I cast spells so that the various robes and bowls flew up;
this was merely to test your arts. He then ordered that Master Chou’s robes and bowl be brought and given to him, yet the spells had no effect on them at all.
An imperial edict ordered ten men to lift it, yet it would not budge. When soldiers were added to move it, it became even more firmly fixed.
(Regarding the house: Dharmaratna identified the ashes, and Huiyao carved wood [for his image].
Dharmaratna arrived in this land at the same time as Kāśyapa Mātanga. Initially, when Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty dredged the Kunming Pond, they reached the bottom of the earth.
Black ashes were obtained. When Emperor Ming arrived at the palace, he questioned Dongfang Shuo about them. Shuo said, "I do not know; you may ask the śramaṇas from the Western Regions.

Later, when Dharmaratna (Lan) indeed arrived, the Han court followed up by questioning him. Lan said, "When the world comes to its end, the kalpa-fire burns through everything, reducing all to embers and ashes;

these are those ashes. (The characters "至明帝" [arrived at Emperor Ming] are redundant. In the *Shamen benzhuan* [Biographies of Śramaṇas], "barbarian" [胡人] is given as the correct term for him; perhaps this current text contains a scribal error.)
Huiyao was a disciple of Master Huiyuan. He resided at Mount Lu and was proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning. He was particularly gifted in ingenious craftsmanship.
As there were no water clocks (leke) in the mountains, he carved wooden lotus flowers with twelve petals from the spring water;

as they rotated with the flowing waves, they determined the twelve hours of the day with such precision that the shadow measurements did not deviate. He also carved wooden geese that could fly several hundred paces.
Yan (the character for "goose" [鵝] appears as "kite" [鳶] in the commentary).
Lingzang wore commoner’s clothes; Fayun wore brocade robes.
After Lingzang entered the Way, he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka deeply and possessed great integrity. He served as a commoner to Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty.

Friend, the High Ancestor (Emperor Wen) again treated him with the rites due to a teacher. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, during a severe drought, the Emperor led the people to Luozhou to offer prayers.
The Emperor traveled together with [Dao]zang and saw that the people were turning toward Zang in great numbers.
He remarked, "I am a layman, a Son of Heaven; the Vinaya Master is a monk, a Son of Heaven."

Fayun was the title of Wanhui; by imperial decree, he was granted the rank of Duke Fayun. From childhood, he was dull-witted and wandered aimlessly from east to west, causing his neighbors to laugh at him;
consequently, he called himself "Wan-hui" (Ten-Thousand-Turns). From that time on, he became known by this name.

When he was ten years old, he learned that his elder brother had been stationed in Liao Yang for a long time without any news. His parents were deeply concerned and held a vegetarian feast to offer prayers. Suddenly, Wanhui said to his mother:
He said, "Brother, you are extremely easy to understand; why worry about it? Then, during the time for the monastic meal, he took his leave of his mother and departed through the gate.
It was not until late evening that he returned, bringing his brother’s letter to his mother. When asked about the circumstances of his journey, he gave no reply at all.
He had traveled from Wenxiang in Guozhou to Liaoyang, a distance of over ten thousand li. Later, when his brother returned, he recounted the details in full.

On that day, he conversed with him and took some cakes to eat together before departing. His parents were greatly astonished and marveled at this. When people learned of it, they sought him out to become a monk;

the Emperor bestowed upon him garments of brocade and silk, which the officials provided for his maintenance. (Regarding the phrase "seeing his elder brother," it means "seeing [the one who was] his elder brother while he was still alive.
Is the character "jiàn" (see) perhaps a scribal error for another character? From then on, it was transmitted as "yīn'ěr" (therefore).)
Regarding Huiyao: Qingniu and Tanhong. Huiyao possessed integrity and discipline from his youth.

He was profoundly learned in the sūtras and śāstras, and his mastery of their meanings was considered preeminent. Qi Zhou Yong, Shen Yue, Chu Yuan, Wang Jian, and others all knew him well and held him in high esteem.
They formed a bond with him as fellow practitioners of the Way. Later, when he passed away, the Son of Heaven attended his funeral, as did the feudal lords.
When the time for the funeral approached, on the evening before the burial, he harnessed the blue ox he had ridden to the coffin and led it away.
Suddenly, the blue ox bellowed and shed tears like rain; though whipped, it would not move. On the following day, the ox returned to the burial site, crying out piteously and shedding tears.
After a short while, a pair of white cranes descended, circled the tomb, and let out mournful cries.
Tanhong was a monk who specialized exclusively in the Vinaya. He frequently resided in mountain forests. Later, at Huanglong Mountain, he piled up firewood and set himself ablaze.
When the people of the valley below attempted to rescue him, they saw that half of his body had already been scorched and charred. After a short while, he burned his entire body again;
both monastics and laypeople alike beheld Tanhong’s body turning entirely golden as he mounted a golden deer and galloped westward.
A True Record of the Inscription on the Mother’s Spirit Banner by Zhi Tandi.

Zhi Tandi was originally a native of Kangju. During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, he moved to reside in China. Tandi’s father served as the Vice Governor of Jizhou, and his mother was surnamed Huang.
While she was napping during the day, she dreamed of a monk who called out to her, Huang, and gave her a fly-whisk (*chūwei*) along with an iron [object].
He wrote two talismans and placed them in his sleeves. Upon waking, both objects were still there. Consequently, he conceived the realization that this was a true dream.
When Tandi was five years old, his mother showed him a fly-whisk and other items. Tandi said, "These were given to me by the King of Qin. His mother asked, "Where did you put them?"
He replied, "I do not remember. When he reached the age of ten, he left home and attained self-realization through the Buddha’s teachings.
He followed his mother to Guanzhong and met the monk Daoshi. Suddenly, [Daoci] called out Daoshi’s name. Daoshi said, "Child, why do you call an elder by name?
Daoci replied, "Just now I suddenly said, 'The Master is Daoci the śrāmaṇera. Daoci was gathering vegetables for the assembly when he was gored by a wild boar. Daoshi—
At first, he did not remember it. He then went to the parents of Daodi and questioned them.

The father recounted the beginning and end of the matter in detail and showed him the writing tablet and the fly-whisk. Jie then wept and said, "This is none other than our late teacher, Master Hongjue.

When the master was lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* for Yao Chang, I served as the assistant lecturer (*dougǎng*). Yao Chang presented these two items to the master; these are they. At the time the master passed away..."

It was precisely the day for consigning the belongings. She further recalled the incident regarding the gathering of vegetables. (In the "Han Ling" [section], the character "Emperor" is absent in one version. Furthermore, this serves to cite the deeds of her ancestors.
Senglun’s surname was Lü; she was a native of Weizhou. Her father, Xun, served as the Governor of Muling.

Before she had conceived, while her parents were seated, there suddenly appeared a foreign monk with bushy eyebrows and white hair, flanked by two attendants holding banners on either side, who said: "We wish to become..."
As for his mother and son: it is not yet known how it was that they suddenly vanished, whereupon she became pregnant.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, at the hour of the fourth watch, she gave birth to Lun; there were two banners flanking him on either side, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. Once he was born, they vanished.
When he reached the age of five, he went with his father to Yunmen Temple, where he met the Master Xian-tong and Chan Master Min.

He then sought to leave the household life. When his two teachers questioned him, he related in detail their extraordinary signs. The two teachers sighed and said, "This child is truly one who may be delivered.
(Omitted: Zhi Xuan departed the country; Kumārajīva entered the Pass.)

Zhixuan entered the monastic order in his youth and studied the scriptural teachings. During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, when Buddhism was suppressed, Zhixuan opposed this with extraordinary resolve, desiring to restore the faith to its former glory.
The Emperor grew enraged and attempted to compel him into marriage. Zhixuan and the other monks remained steadfast, refusing to change their resolve.

Consequently, the Emperor issued an edict for Zhixuan to participate in the administration of state affairs. Zhixuan fled the capital city, intending to travel to the capital of Qi. At that time, due to the [fall of] Qi...

The border regions were all covered with spears and brambles, such that no one could pass through. There was a wealthy old woman in Qi surnamed Zhang who, seeing Huian’s lofty and extraordinary character, spread out carpets for thirty li and had Huian tread across them to reach Qi, where he would once again propagate the Great Teaching.
Kumārajīva, translated here as "Child-Longevity," was a native of India. His family had been hereditary ministers of state for generations.

His father, Kumārabhīta, later also entered the monastic order. His mother was the younger sister of the King of Kucha. While Kumārajīva was still in his mother’s womb, she suddenly became exceptionally wise and insightful, far surpassing her usual capacity;

however, after his birth, she forgot what she had previously understood. When Kumārajīva reached the age of nine, he possessed great intellectual acuity and eloquence regarding the Buddhist teachings. From [the age of nine], the Buddhist teachings...
The King honored him with great reverence, whereupon his fame resounded throughout the eastern lands. At that time, Fu Jian heard of this and said:
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in Kucha and Shi Dao’an in Xiangyang; I long for them both.
These monks of great sagehood are truly the treasures of the state. He then led seventy thousand troops westward to invade Kucha and captured Kumārajīva.
Fu Jian and his ministers welcomed him into Guanzhong, where he greatly propagated the teachings of the Dharma (Fu Jian and his ministers likely refer to Yao Xing of Later Qin).
Dharmodgata crossed the mountain pass; Fahu ascended the mountain.
Dharmodgata—translated here as Fayong—initially departed from this land with twenty-five people, including Tanlang, leaving behind their footprints here.
Traveling far to the Western Heaven, he passed through the Pamir Mountains. The ice and snow were piercingly cold, and the miasmic vapors were dark and oppressive.

Below lay a great river flowing as swiftly as an arrow, washing against the flanks of both eastern and western mountains. They fashioned a bridge by fastening ropes together; ten men would go there to raise smoke as a signal.
Later, when they saw smoke rising as before, they knew they had passed through safely; if no smoke was seen, they knew it was dark.
The wind blew them down into the river. Later, they again crossed the Great Snow Mountains. There were precipitous cliffs standing sheer with no place to set foot;
on the walls of the cliffs were old wooden pegs, each pair facing one another at regular intervals.

Each man took hold of four pegs, first pulling out the lower one and then grasping the upper one with his hand, passing the load from one to the next in turn. It took three days to cross, using rock honey as their provisions, yet all their companions perished.
On the road, he took only the scriptures and managed to return to this land.
Fahu was a fellow student of Dao’an; later, having clarified the principles of Buddhism, he led his followers into Shu during the chaos caused by Shi Hu.
Parting from Master An at Jinyu Valley, he climbed to the summit of the mountain and gazed into the distance with sorrowful lamentation:
"This mountain rises high and many are those who roam its peaks; yet once parted from this place, where will one ultimately go? Master An replied, "The Master maintains his mind with focused intent."
What need is there to fear future births? If wisdom does not sprout, that is truly pitiable. (End of the separate section;
the *Biàn* [Transformation] version reads "End of the *Huà*" [Transformation]).

(Recorded by Han) Paramārtha, whose name means "Ultimate Truth," was originally from Western India. He came to reside in the South... [text continues with details regarding his arrival and reliance on patrons].
At the seashore, there was at that time the Regional Inspector, Lord Ou-yang Mu, who held him in profound esteem and requested that he reside at Chih-chi Temple.
T’i sometimes stayed at a private villa on a small island surrounded by water, cut off from the four directions. Lord Mu’s son, Hsüeh-ho, wished to go and pay his respects;

however, as the waves were rising high upon the island, he did not dare venture across. T’i then spread out his sitting mat upon the water and crossed over with effortless ease, reaching his destination.
Having already reached the bank, his sitting mat remained dry. When the time for the tide to recede approached, he crossed back alone upon a lotus leaf; none could fathom his spiritual power.
As for Wuxiang, it was unknown where he came from. He resided at a mountain temple in Fuzhou, upstream on the great river, where waves and billows rose continuously.
Without a boat, one could not cross to that temple. The method was simply to place plantain leaves upon the water and tread upon them to cross.
At times, they would place an alms bowl in the water and have someone step on it; thus, they would reach the shore with effortless ease.
(End) Shen Shifu (The Spirit Who Subdues Well). Huiwei asked the ghost Shen about Shifu. His other name was Dengzhao.
After entering the Way, he practiced dhyāna and contemplation on Mount Sangzi. A mountain spirit sought to submit and receive the precepts.
